intro.carita: Uttama Carita (the third episode, chapters 5–13), in which this chapter turns from the battles to the gods’ thanksgiving. In the recitation tradition its presiding form is Mahāsarasvatī; this is the Gita Press viniyoga (printed before chapter 5), not a statement of the Purāṇa text. In the Gita Press pāṭha chapter 11 has no viniyoga of its own, only a dhyāna, of Bhuvaneśī: ‘I worship Bhuvaneśī, bright as the rising sun, crowned with the moon, high-breasted, three-eyed, smiling, her hands showing the boon, the goad, the noose and the gesture that dispels fear’ (बालरविद्युतिमिन्दुकिरीटां … वरदाङ्कुशपाशाभीतिकरां प्रभजे भुवनेशीम्). The dhyāna is liturgy; the chapter itself never names Bhuvaneśī.
intro.summary: Śumbha is dead, and the gods, Agni at their head and Indra among them, their faces shining like opened lotuses, praise the Goddess as Kātyāyanī (11.2). They ask her grace as the refuge of the afflicted, the mother of the world and its sovereign (11.3); they name her the earth that supports the world and the waters that nourish it (11.4), Viṣṇu’s power and the supreme Māyā, by whom the world is bewildered and who, when gracious, is the cause of liberation (11.5); and they confess that no praise can reach one whose forms are all knowledge and all women (11.6–7). Then the refrain begins, नारायणि नमोऽस्तु ते: she is understanding in every heart, time and its changes, the blessing of all that is blessed, the power of creation, continuance and destruction, the rescuer of those who come for refuge (11.8–12); the nine powers who fought in chapters 8–9, Brahmāṇī to Cāmuṇḍā, are each saluted as Nārāyaṇī (11.13–21); and so are Lakṣmī, Modesty, Faith and the rest, Great Night and, in the Gita Press reading, Great Nescience (11.22–23). Under the name Durgā the refrain becomes a prayer for protection from fear (11.24), and her gentle face, her trident, her bell and her sword are asked to guard the gods (11.25–28). In the longer metres again they praise her power over illness and desire and the refuge she gives (11.29), ask who but she could have become many to destroy the asuras (11.30), and who but she dwells in all knowledge and whirls the world in the dark pit of ‘mine’ (11.31); she stands guard wherever danger is (11.32–33), and they ask her to keep them from fear and calamity and to be the giver of boons (11.34–35). The Goddess offers a boon that will benefit the worlds (11.36–37); the gods ask that every affliction of the three worlds be quelled and their enemies destroyed in just this way (11.38–39). Her answer is a prophecy (11.40–55): in the twenty-eighth age of Vaivasvata Manu a second Śumbha and Niśumbha will be born, and she, born of Yaśodā in the house of Nanda and dwelling on the Vindhya, will destroy them (11.41–42); descending in a terrible form she will devour the Dānavas of Vipracitti’s line and be called Raktadantikā, the Red-toothed (11.43–45); in a hundred-year drought, born of no womb, she will look on the sages with a hundred eyes as Śatākṣī, feed the world with plants from her own body as Śākambharī, and slay the asura Durgama, so that her name will be Durgā (11.46–50); on the Himālaya she will devour the rākṣasas as Bhīmā (11.50–52); against Aruṇa she will take a form of countless bees as Bhrāmarī (11.52–54); and whenever the Dānavas oppress the world, she will descend and destroy the enemies (11.54–55).
intro.forms: Kātyāyanī, the name under which the gods begin and return to their praise (11.2, 11.25); Viśveśvarī, the sovereign of the universe (11.3, 11.33); Vaiṣṇavī śakti and the supreme Māyā (11.5); Ambā and Ambikā, the Mother (11.6, 11.30); Nārāyaṇī, the name of the refrain (11.8–23), joined in one verse with Śiva’s consort as Śivā, Tryambakā and Gaurī (11.10); the nine forms who fought in chapters 8–9 — Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Aindrī, Śivadūtī and Cāmuṇḍā (11.13–21); the powers Lakṣmī, Lajjā, Mahāvidyā, Śraddhā, Puṣṭi, Svadhā, Dhruvā, Mahārātri and Mahā-avidyā (11.22), Medhā, Sarasvatī, Bhūti, Bābhravī, Tāmasī and Niyati (11.23); Durgā, Bhadrakālī and Caṇḍikā in the prayers for protection (11.24, 11.26, 11.28); Varadā, the giver of boons, the gods’ word and her own (11.35, 11.37). In the prophecy: the daughter of Yaśodā who dwells on the Vindhya (11.42), Raktadantikā (11.45), Śatākṣī (11.47), Śākambharī (11.49), Durgā (11.50), Bhīmā (11.52) and Bhrāmarī (11.54).
intro.significance: This is the fourth of the Devī Māhātmya’s great hymns, after Brahmā’s (1.73–87) and the gods’ hymns of chapters 4 and 5, and from its refrain it is known as the Nārāyaṇī Stuti; it is often recited by itself, and its verse सर्वमङ्गलमङ्गल्ये (11.10) is perhaps the most widely recited line of the whole text. The hymn gathers what the battles showed: the Mothers who fought in chapters 8–9 are saluted one by one as forms of the one Nārāyaṇī (11.13–21), and the gods’ question ‘who else?’ (11.30) echoes the Goddess’s own ‘who else is there besides me?’ (10.5). The chapter also turns the story from the past to the future. The gods ask not for one more rescue but that their enemies be destroyed ‘in just this way’ (11.39), and the Goddess answers with a promise that runs into later ages — into the time of Kṛṣṇa (11.41–42) and through five descents — and ends as a rule: whenever oppression arises, she will descend (11.54–55). Along the way the prophecy gives the name Durgā its story (11.49–50). Her speech continues into chapter 12.
intro.grammar: The hymn is built of vocatives, and the chapter is the best place in the text to learn them: ī-stems shorten the final vowel (नारायणि, गौरि, लक्ष्मि, ऐन्द्रि), ā-stems end in -e (शिवे, लज्जे, श्रद्धे, चामुण्डे), i-stems take guṇa (शक्ते, नियते), and two stem-form vocatives, पुष्टि and भूति (11.22–23), are kept as printed. Most vocatives are compounds — upapada tatpuruṣas of the agent in -हरा, -दा, -धरा, -धारिणी, -प्रदायिनी and bahuvrīhis of weapon and mount — and an instrumental of form stands among them (माहेश्वरीस्वरूपेण, 11.14; नृसिंहरूपेणोग्रेण, 11.18; शिवदूतीस्वरूपेण, 11.20). The refrain is नमः अस्तु ते, the third-person imperative of √अस् with the dative. Prayers use the imperative (प्रसीद, पाहि, त्राहि, परिपालय, नय) and the third-person imperative of blessing (पातु, भवतु), with the danger in the ablative (भयेभ्यः, 11.24; भीतेः, 11.26; पापेभ्यः, 11.27) and the purpose in the dative (शुभाय, 11.28). Rhetorical questions with का carry the confessions of 11.6–7, 11.30 and 11.31. The gods’ request uses the gerundive with an instrumental agent (त्वया कार्यम्, 11.39). The prophecy is in the future tense throughout (उत्पत्स्येते, नाशयिष्यामि, हनिष्यामि, सम्भविष्यामि, भरिष्यामि, स्तोष्यन्ति, करिष्यामि), with Purāṇic forms (वधिष्यामि, 11.49, 11.53; the parasmaipada निरीक्षिष्यामि, 11.47; the ordinal अष्टाविंशतिमे, 11.41), names given with इति and a double accusative (मां … रक्तदन्तिकाम्, 11.45), and correlative clauses that run across verses (यदा … तदा, 11.50–51 and 11.52–53; the distributive यदा यदा … तदा तदा, 11.54–55).
intro.teaching: Literally, the gods thank the Goddess who has saved them, she offers a boon, and she foretells the forms in which she will come again. As teaching, the Śākta tradition reads the hymn as a summary of the whole text: every power — of each god (the Mothers, 11.13–21), of knowledge and of women (11.6), of time (11.9), of creation, continuance and destruction (11.11) — is one Goddess, and the refrain gives Viṣṇu’s name, Nārāyaṇī, to the consort of Śiva (11.10). The same power binds and frees: she is the Māyā that bewilders and, when gracious, the cause of liberation (11.5), the lamp of discernment and the darkness of ‘mine’ (11.31). The hymn begins and ends with grace to those who come for refuge (11.3, 11.35), and says that those who take refuge in her become a refuge for others (11.29, 11.33). The tradition compares the closing promise (11.54–55) with the Bhagavadgītā’s promise of descent (4.7–8); the chapter itself names no such source. These readings are the tradition’s, and the commentary presents them as such; the chapter’s own words are a hymn and a prophecy.
themes: Nārāyaṇī: the powers of all the gods as one Goddess
Refuge given, and refuge passed on
The power that binds is the power that frees
Gentle face and fierce weapons, both for protection
The boon that becomes a promise of descent
Names given by those she saves

conclusion.narrative: With Śumbha dead the battles are over, and the chapter is given to the gods’ thanksgiving. Their hymn, the Nārāyaṇī Stuti, names the Goddess as the ground and nourishment of the world, as Viṣṇu’s power and Māyā, and, verse after verse, as Nārāyaṇī in every form she took in the war; it asks her protection, and ends by asking her to be the giver of boons (11.2–35). She offers a boon; the gods ask that the worlds be freed of affliction and their enemies destroyed as they have just been (11.37–39). She answers with the promise of five future descents — as the daughter of Yaśodā on the Vindhya, as Raktadantikā, as Śatākṣī, Śākambharī and Durgā, as Bhīmā and as Bhrāmarī — and with a rule: whenever the Dānavas oppress the world, she will come down and destroy the enemies (11.41–55).

‘be gracious’, the hymn’s first and last prayer
one who has come for refuge
the power that bewilders the world

constructions: The refrain: a chain of vocatives closed by नमः अस्तु ते, the imperative of √अस् with the dative (11.8–23); it changes to Durgā (11.24), Kātyāyanī (11.25) and Bhadrakālī (11.26), and to the statement त्वां नता वयम् (11.28).
Vocatives by stem: ī-stems shorten (नारायणि, गौरि, लक्ष्मि), ā-stems end in -e (शिवे, लज्जे), i-stems take guṇa (शक्ते, नियते); पुष्टि and भूति are stem-form vocatives kept as printed (11.22–23).
An instrumental of form among the vocatives (माहेश्वरीस्वरूपेण, 11.14; नृसिंहरूपेणोग्रेण, 11.18; शिवदूतीस्वरूपेण, 11.20).
Prayer in the imperative, with the danger in the ablative and the purpose in the dative (त्राहि … भयेभ्यः, 11.24; पातु नो भीतेः, 11.26; शुभाय … भवतु, 11.28).
Rhetorical questions with का in place of a denial (का ते स्तुतिः, 11.6; तत्प्रकरोति कान्या, 11.30; का त्वदन्या, 11.31).
The gerundive of obligation with an instrumental agent (त्वया कार्यम्, 11.39), and with a genitive agent (त्रैलोक्यवासिनाम् ईड्ये, 11.35).
The future of prophecy, including Purāṇic forms (वधिष्यामि, 11.49, 11.53; निरीक्षिष्यामि, 11.47), and names given with इति or a double accusative (11.45, 11.47, 11.49, 11.54).
Correlative clauses carried across verses: यदा … तदा (11.50–51, 11.52–53) and the distributive यदा यदा … तदा तदा (11.54–55).
insights: The many are one: each of the Mothers who fought in chapters 8–9 is saluted as Nārāyaṇī (11.13–21), and the gods’ ‘who else could do this?’ (11.30) answers the Goddess’s own claim to be alone (10.5).

The power that bewilders is the power that frees: she is the supreme Māyā and, when gracious, the cause of liberation (11.5); she is in every lamp of discernment and whirls the world in the pit of ‘mine’ (11.31); and, in the Gita Press reading, she is both Mahāvidyā and Mahā-avidyā (11.22).
All knowledge and every woman are her forms, and she alone fills the world (11.6): the verse from which the Śākta tradition draws its reverence for women as forms of the Goddess.

Her gentle and her terrible forms are one protection: the gentle three-eyed face is asked first, then the flaming trident, the bell and the bloodied sword (11.25–28); her pleasure takes away illness, her anger every cherished hope (11.29).
Refuge becomes refuge-giving: those who take refuge in her become a refuge themselves (11.29), and those who bow to her become the shelter of the universe (11.33).
Her grace is a standing promise, not a single act: the gods ask for ‘just this way’ (11.39), and she promises to descend whenever oppression arises (11.54–55).
conclusion.srividya: The one specific connection is liturgical, not in the Purāṇa text: the Gita Press dhyāna before this chapter meditates on Bhuvaneśī — Bhuvaneśvarī, a name the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also gives the Goddess (294, भुवनेश्वरी) — three-eyed (compare 453, त्रिनयना), smiling, and holding the noose and the goad, two of the four weapons the Lalitā Sahasranāma gives Lalitā (8, रागस्वरूपपाशाढ्या; 9, क्रोधाकाराङ्कुशोज्ज्वला). In the hymn the parallels are names and ideas: नारायणी (298), the name of the refrain; स्वर्गापवर्गदा (764, compare 11.8); सर्वमङ्गला (200, compare 11.10); विद्याऽविद्यास्वरूपिणी (402), which states in one name what 11.22 states by pairing महाविद्ये and, in the Gita Press reading, महाऽविद्ये; विश्वभ्रमणकारिणी (889) and ममताहन्त्री (165), the two sides of 11.31; and कराङ्गुलिनखोत्पन्ननारायणदशाकृतिः (80), Viṣṇu’s avatāras coming from the Goddess, beside the Boar and the Man-Lion of 11.17–18. In the prophecy विन्ध्याचलनिवासिनी (11.42) is also a name there in the identical form (336), and दुर्गमा and दुर्गा stand side by side (189, 190), though the Lalitā Sahasranāma does not tell the story of Durgama (11.49–50). The Mothers of 11.13–21 overlap with the eight Mothers honoured in the outer square of the Śrīcakra (see chapter 8), a separate liturgical tradition. These are shared Śākta names and images, not evidence that one text depends on the other; the chapter itself states no specifically Śrīvidyā doctrine.

key_verses.why: You are Viṣṇu’s power, the seed of the universe, the supreme Māyā: by you the world is bewildered, and, gracious, you are the cause of liberation on earth.
All forms of knowledge and all women in the worlds are your forms; you alone, the Mother, fill this world — what praise can there be of you?
सर्वमङ्गलमङ्गल्ये — Śivā, Tryambakā, Gaurī saluted as Nārāyaṇī: the most widely recited verse of the hymn.
Form of all, Lady of all, endowed with every power: protect us from fears, Durgā Devī — the refrain turns to a prayer for protection.
Pleased, you remove every illness; angered, every cherished hope; those who take refuge in you meet no misfortune and become a refuge themselves.
Who but you dwells in all knowledge and the lamps of discernment — and who but you whirls this world in the dark pit of ‘mine’?
With 11.54: whenever oppression born of the Dānavas arises, each time I shall descend and destroy the enemies.

sandhi_patterns: The refrain’s नमोऽस्तु (नमः + अस्तु: -aḥ → -o, then pūrvarūpa) closes every verse from 11.8 to 11.26.

Visarga sandhi throughout: -aḥ → -o before voiced sounds (नो देवि, 11.24, 11.27; खड्गो भवतु, 11.28; ततो मां, 11.45), -āḥ → -ā (सुरा वह्नि-, 11.2; सकला जगत्सु, 11.6; देवा ऊचुः, 11.38), visarga → s/ś before t/c (भयेभ्यस्त्राहि, 11.24; ततस्तौ, 11.42; भूयश्च, 11.46) and → r after other vowels (तुष्टुवुरिष्टलाभाद्, 11.2; मातर्जगतः, 11.3; रूपैरनेकैर्बहुधा, 11.30; भीतेर्भद्रकालि, 11.26).

Vowel sandhi of every kind: savarṇa-dīrgha (स्थितासि, 11.4; वरदाहं, 11.37; शाकम्भरीति, 11.49), guṇa (विश्वस्योपरतौ, 11.9; प्रसीदेशे, 11.23; यन्मनसेच्छथ, 11.37), vṛddhi (त्वयैकया, 11.6; चैन्द्रि, 11.19; तत्रैव, 11.49), yaṇ (देव्युवाच, 11.36, 11.40; विवेकदीपेष्वाद्येषु across the printed line, 11.31; करिष्याम्यरिसंक्षयम्, 11.55) and pūrvarūpa (महाशक्तिधरेऽनघे, 11.15; ममत्वगर्तेऽतिमहान्धकारे, 11.31; वैवस्वतेऽन्तरे, 11.41).

Consonant sandhi: t → n before a nasal (विपन्नराणाम्, 11.29; यन्मुनीन्, 11.47; तन्मे, 11.50, 11.52), final n → ṃś/ṃs before c/t (उत्पातपाकजनितांश्च, 11.34; वैप्रचित्तांस्तु, 11.43), t → d before a voiced sound (इष्टलाभाद् विकाशि-, 11.2).
One declared hiatus: प्राप्ते | अष्टाविंशतिमे at the pāda break of 11.41; the vowels also stand apart at the half-verse break of 11.34 (नयाशु | उत्पात-).

The Gita Press marks avagrahas where no letter is lost or where the vowel is long (महाऽविद्ये, 11.22; पापेभ्योऽनः, 11.27; बहुधाऽऽत्ममूर्तिम्, 11.30; कृत्वाऽसंख्येय-, 11.53); the padaccheda follows the grammar.
samasa: Upapada tatpuruṣas of the agent make most of the hymn’s epithets: -हरा/-हारिणी (प्रपन्नार्तिहरे, 11.3; वृत्रप्राणहरे, 11.19; विश्वार्तिहारिणि, 11.35), -दा/-प्रदायिनी (स्वर्गापवर्गदे, 11.8; परिणामप्रदायिनि, 11.9; वरदा, 11.35, 11.37), -धरा/-धारिणी (ब्रह्माणीरूपधारिणि, 11.13; त्रिशूलचन्द्राहिधरे, 11.14), and the names शाकम्भरी (with the inserted m, 11.49) and विन्ध्याचलनिवासिनी (11.42).

Bahuvrīhis picture the Mothers by weapon, mount and face (शङ्खचक्रगदाशार्ङ्गगृहीतपरमायुधे, 11.16; दंष्ट्रोद्धृतवसुंधरे, 11.17; दंष्ट्राकरालवदने, शिरोमालाविभूषणे, 11.21) and give the future names (रक्तदन्तिका, 11.45; शताक्षी, 11.47; असंख्येयषट्पदम्, 11.53).
Long nested compounds, two of them filling a whole printed line (शरणागतदीनार्तपरित्राणपरायणे, 11.12; विकाशिवक्त्राब्जविकाशिताशाः, 11.2), and असुरासृग्वसापङ्कचर्चितः (11.28).

Karmadhārayas with महा- (महासुर, 11.2, 11.30, 11.41; महाविद्या, महारात्रि, महाऽविद्या, 11.22), rūpakas (वक्त्राब्ज, 11.2; ममत्वगर्त, 11.31) and karmadhārayas with भूत ‘being’ (आधारभूता, 11.4; सर्वभूता, 11.7; शक्तिभूते, 11.11).
Dvandvas (चराचर, samāhāra, 11.3; स्वर्गापवर्ग, 11.8; सृष्टिस्थितिविनाशानाम्, 11.11; मयूरकुक्कुट, 11.15) and negative compounds (अनघे, 11.15; अनावृष्ट्याम्, अनम्भसि, अयोनिजा, 11.46).
grammar_notes: पुष्टि (11.22) and भूति (11.23) are stem-form vocatives for पुष्टे and भूते, kept as printed; the printed पुष्टिस्वधे is divided as two vocatives.
शक्ते (11.9) can belong to शक्ति ‘power’ or शक्ता ‘able’; it is read as शक्ति, as in 11.5 and 11.11. नियते (11.23) is read as Niyati, with नियता ‘the self-restrained’ as the alternative.
स्तव्यपरा परोक्तिः (11.6) is read as a definition of praise in apposition to स्तुतिः; the reading as epithets of the Goddess is flagged.
In 11.27 the printed पापेभ्योऽनः is read as पापेभ्यः + नः, and the second नः as genitive with पापेभ्यः (‘from our sins’).
-रूपेण/-स्वरूपेण in 11.14, 11.18 and 11.20 are instrumentals of form standing among vocatives, not vocatives.
यत् … तम् (11.37) has a neuter relative and a masculine correlative, read as a generic ‘whatever (boon)’.
Purāṇic forms in the prophecy: the ordinal अष्टाविंशतिमे (11.41), the parasmaipada future निरीक्षिष्यामि of an ātmanepadin root (11.47) and the future वधिष्यामि (11.49, 11.53).
The printed आवृष्टेः (11.48) is divided as आ + वृष्टेः, ‘until the rain’.
themes: Nārāyaṇī and the one Goddess of many forms
The boon and the promise of descent

mantras.anvaya: तत्र देव्या महासुरेन्द्रे हते (सति), इष्टलाभात् विकाशिवक्त्राब्जविकाशिताशाः वह्निपुरोगमाः सेन्द्राः सुराः तां कात्यायनीं तुष्टुवुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: A locative absolute sets the time (देव्या हते … महासुरेन्द्रे); the main clause is सुराः … तुष्टुवुः with its object तां कात्यायनीम्; इष्टलाभात् gives the cause and the long bahuvrīhi describes the gods.
mantras.lit: When the great lord of the asuras had been slain there by the Goddess, the gods together with Indra, led by Vahni, praised that Kātyāyanī, because they had gained their desire — they whose radiant lotus-faces made the quarters bright.
mantras.tr: When the Goddess had slain the mighty lord of the asuras, the gods, with Indra among them and Agni at their head, their faces shining like opened lotuses and lighting up every quarter for joy at their wish fulfilled, sang the praise of Kātyāyanī.
mantras.tr_note: ‘For joy’ renders the ablative of cause इष्टलाभात् (‘because of gaining what they wished’), which the bright faces express.

comm.t: The narrative frame of the hymn. Śumbha has fallen (10.27); the gods, led by Agni and with Indra among them, praise the Goddess under the name Kātyāyanī, the name she already bore on the battlefield (8.29). Their joy is pictured in their faces, which shine like opened lotuses and light up the directions. Verses 11.2–6 are in upajāti (lines of indravajrā and upendravajrā, eleven syllables).

This is the fourth of the great hymns of the Devī Māhātmya, after Brahmā’s hymn (1.73–87), the gods’ hymn in chapter 4 and the hymn of chapter 5. From its refrain नारायणि नमोऽस्तु ते (11.8 onward) it is known as the Nārāyaṇī Stuti, and it is often recited by itself. Agni at the head of the gods recalls his Vedic role as their priest and messenger; the text itself gives no reason.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also names the Goddess Kātyāyanī (name 556, कात्यायनी). The name is traditionally connected with the sage Kātyāyana; the Devī Māhātmya does not explain it. The two texts are separate works.

flags.uncertain: विकाशि-/विकाशित- are printed with ś (वि + √काश् ‘to shine’). Printings often write विकासि-/विकासित- with s (वि + √कस् ‘to open, blossom’), and the two spellings are frequently confused in manuscripts. The Gita Press reading is kept; either root gives the image of faces opening and shining like lotuses.

mantras.anvaya_en: Four short sentences, three of them prayers in the imperative (प्रसीद, प्रसीद, प्रसीद … पाहि), each with its own vocative; the last is a statement with असि understood.
mantras.lit: O Goddess, remover of the distress of those who take refuge, be gracious! Be gracious, O Mother of the whole world! Be gracious, O Sovereign of the universe; protect the universe! You, O Goddess, are the ruler of the moving and the unmoving.
mantras.tr: O Goddess, who take away the sorrow of all who come to you for refuge, be gracious! Be gracious, Mother of the whole world! Be gracious, Queen of the universe, and protect it! For you, O Goddess, are sovereign over all that moves and all that is still.
mantras.tr_note: ‘For’ makes explicit the link the last line has with the prayers before it; the Sanskrit simply states it.

comm.t: The hymn opens with a threefold prayer, प्रसीद, ‘be gracious’, and each time names the Goddess by a relation: to those who seek refuge, to the world as its mother, to the universe as its sovereign. The last line gives the ground of the prayer: she rules all that moves and all that does not.

The first epithet, प्रपन्नार्तिहरा, puts the hymn’s theme at its head: she is first approached as the one who takes away the distress of the प्रपन्न, those who have come to her for shelter. The theme returns in the refrain verse 11.12 (शरणागतदीनार्तपरित्राणपरायणे) and in the gods’ closing prayer for protection (11.24–28, 11.34–35).

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the names ईश्वरी (271) and चराचरजगन्नाथा (244), ‘ruler of the moving and unmoving world’, which say what the last line of this verse says. The likeness is shared Śākta vocabulary; the two texts are separate works.
A modern reading: the gods have just been rescued, yet their first word is not thanks but ‘be gracious’. Gratitude here takes the form of asking to remain under the same care.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: the first states that she alone is the support of the world and gives the reason in a यतः clause; the second, with the intransitive verb आप्यायते, says the whole world is nourished through her as water. The vocative stands at the end.
mantras.lit: You alone are the support of the world, since you abide in the form of the earth. By you, abiding in the form of the waters, this whole (world) is nourished, O you whose might cannot be overcome.
mantras.tr: You alone are the ground on which the world rests, for you abide as the earth. And as the waters you nourish this whole world, O Goddess of invincible power.
mantras.tr_note: The tr turns ‘by you … this whole is nourished’ into an active sentence (‘you nourish’); the vocative is rendered ‘O Goddess of invincible power’.

comm.t: The gods name two of the elements as her forms. As earth she holds the world up; as water she makes it swell and thrive. The word यतः makes the first line a reason: she is the world’s support because she is the earth.

The verse continues the teaching of Brahmā’s hymn, that the Goddess is not only the power behind the world but its very substance (1.76: त्वयैतत्पाल्यते, ‘by you this is protected’). Earth and water are named because they are the ground and the nourishment of life; the tradition reads them as standing for all the elements.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the names मही (718), ‘the earth’, and सर्वाधारा (659), ‘the support of all’. The agreement is in shared Śākta vocabulary; the two texts are separate works.
A modern reading: the ground under one’s feet and the water one drinks are named here as the Goddess herself. Reverence begins with what is most ordinary and most needed.

A tatpuruṣa keeps the gender of its last member: हेतु is masculine, so ‘you (f.) are the cause’ is त्वं … मुक्तिहेतुः, as in 4.9 (या मुक्तिहेतुः).

mantras.anvaya: त्वम् अनन्तवीर्या वैष्णवी शक्तिः (असि)। (त्वं) विश्वस्य बीजं परमा माया असि। (हे) देवि, एतत् समस्तं (त्वया) सम्मोहितम्। त्वं वै प्रसन्ना (सती) भुवि मुक्तिहेतुः (भवसि)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Four predications about the Goddess: Viṣṇu’s power, the seed of the world, the supreme Māyā (verb असि), and, when gracious, the cause of liberation. Between them stands the effect of her Māyā: the whole world is bewildered.
mantras.lit: You are the power of Viṣṇu, of boundless might; you are the seed of the universe, the supreme Māyā. All this, O Goddess, is held in delusion; you indeed, when pleased, are the cause of liberation on earth.
mantras.tr: You are Viṣṇu’s own power, boundless in might, the seed of the universe, the supreme Māyā. By you, O Goddess, this whole world is held in enchantment; and you, when you are gracious, are the cause of liberation on earth.
mantras.tr_note: ‘By you’ in the third sentence is supplied: the participle सम्मोहितम् implies an agent, and the verse has just named her as Māyā.

comm.t: The verse holds both sides of the Goddess together: as Māyā she keeps the whole world bewildered, and when she is pleased she is the cause of release. Binding and freeing come from the same power.

This is the teaching of the first carita repeated in the gods’ mouths: Mahāmāyā, Hari’s power, bewilders the world (1.55), and when gracious (प्रसन्ना) she becomes the cause of liberation (1.57). ‘Vaiṣṇavī śakti’ recalls the name Viṣṇumāyā under which the gods praised her in chapter 5 (5.14–16).

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the names वैष्णवी (892), विष्णुमाया (339), महामाया (215) and मुक्तिदा (736), ‘giver of liberation’. The names belong to a shared Śākta vocabulary; the two texts are separate works.
A modern reading: what clouds the mind and what clears it are not two rival forces here. The same reality appears as confusion while it is resisted and as freedom once it is met with devotion.

samasa.sense: speech whose whole business is something worth praising — the definition of a hymn
samasa.alt: Also read as a pañcamī tatpuruṣa, स्तव्येभ्यः परा, ‘beyond the things that can be praised’, and referred to the Goddess (‘you who are beyond the praiseworthy’). But the word is nominative and agrees with स्तुतिः, not with the genitive ते; the bahuvrīhi keeps the grammar of the line.

samasa.sense: lofty, excellent speech
samasa.alt: Also read as परा उक्तिः in the sense of ‘the supreme Word’ (the Goddess as speech itself); again the agreement with स्तुतिः favours ‘exalted utterance’.

स्तव्य is a gerundive of √स्तु with -ya (yat): the root vowel takes guṇa (स्तो-) and o becomes av before the y (स्तव्य), ‘to be praised’.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) देवि, समस्ताः विद्याः तव भेदाः (सन्ति); जगत्सु समस्ताः सकलाः स्त्रियः (तव भेदाः)। त्वया एकया अम्बया एतत् पूरितम्। ते का स्तुतिः (स्यात्)? (स्तुतिः हि) स्तव्यपरा परोक्तिः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two nominal sentences (all knowledge, all women are her forms); a passive one (the world is filled by her alone); then a question and, in apposition, what praise is: the last two nominatives define स्तुतिः.
mantras.lit: All branches of knowledge, O Goddess, are your distinct forms; all women in the worlds, every one of them. By you, the one Mother, this (world) is filled. What praise is there of you — (praise being) an exalted utterance directed to what is to be praised?
mantras.tr: Every branch of knowledge, O Goddess, is a form of you, and so is every woman in all the worlds. You alone, the Mother, fill this whole world. What praise can there be of you? Praise is lofty speech about something to be praised.
mantras.tr_note: The last pāda is read as a definition of praise: praise speaks of something as its object, and the verse has just said there is nothing she does not fill. The other reading (‘you who are beyond the praiseworthy, the supreme Word’) is given under Samāsa and in the flags.

comm.t: Every form of knowledge and every woman in every world are named as her own forms, and the whole world is filled by her alone. The verse then asks what praise could be offered to such a one: praise speaks of an object, and there is nothing outside her to speak of.

The Śākta tradition has drawn from this verse its teaching that every woman is to be honoured as a form of the Goddess. The ‘branches of knowledge’ are traditionally understood as all the sciences, sacred and secular. The doubt about praise is a classic theme of hymns: the hymn goes on praising while confessing that praise cannot reach her (compare 4.4 and 4.6, and the close of Brahmā’s hymn, 1.83–85: कस्त्वां स्तोतुमिहेश्वरः).

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the names विद्या (549) and विद्याऽविद्यास्वरूपिणी (402), ‘whose form is both knowledge and ignorance’. The idea is shared Śākta thought; the two texts are separate works.
A modern reading: the verse places the sacred in the women one actually meets and in every honest form of learning. Its reverence is meant to be practised in ordinary life, not kept for the shrine.

flags.uncertain: The last pāda, स्तव्यपरा परोक्तिः, is read in two ways: as a definition of praise in apposition to स्तुतिः (‘an exalted utterance directed to what is to be praised’), followed here because both words are nominative like स्तुतिः; or as epithets of the Goddess (‘beyond the praiseworthy, the supreme Word’), which needs त्वम् to be understood. Both readings are traditional in translation; the point of the verse — no praise can match her — is the same.

An imperative used in a rhetorical question: ‘what loftier words should there be?’ — i.e. none could be.
Dative of स्तुति: i-stems take guṇa before the dative ending (स्तुते + ए → स्तुतये). The dative expresses purpose: ‘for (the sake of) praise’.

mantras.anvaya: यदा सर्वभूता स्वर्गमुक्तिप्रदायिनी देवी त्वं स्तुता (असि), (तदा) स्तुतये काः वा परमोक्तयः भवन्तु?
mantras.anvaya_en: A यदा clause (with तदा understood) and a rhetorical question: once she has been named as all that is and as the giver of heaven and liberation, no further words for praise remain.
mantras.lit: When you, the Goddess who have become all things, the giver of heaven and liberation, are (thus) praised, what supreme utterances could there be for praise?
mantras.tr: When you, the Goddess who are all that is, who grant both heaven and liberation, have been praised as that, what loftier words could be left to praise you?
mantras.tr_note: ‘As that’ makes explicit that the praise consists in the epithets just given; the Sanskrit says only ‘you are praised’. ‘Left’ renders the force of the rhetorical question.

comm.t: The upajāti stanzas end and the anuṣṭubh verses begin. The gods close their first argument: to say that she has become all things, and that she grants both heaven and liberation, is already the whole of praise; no finer words remain.

The verse completes the thought of 11.6. Since everything is her form, naming her as everything is the highest praise. From the next verse the hymn turns from statement to salutation, ending each verse with नारायणि नमोऽस्तु ते.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name स्वर्गापवर्गदा (764), ‘giver of heaven and liberation’, which the next verse here also uses (स्वर्गापवर्गदे, 11.8). The two texts are separate works.

Imperative third person of √अस्: ‘let (homage) be’. With नमः and the dative ते it forms the standard formula of salutation.
Locative of the consonant stem हृद्, which supplies the oblique cases of हृदय ‘heart’.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) सर्वस्य जनस्य हृदि बुद्धिरूपेण संस्थिते, स्वर्गापवर्गदे देवि नारायणि, ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: A chain of vocatives (संस्थिते … स्वर्गापवर्गदे … देवि … नारायणि) and one main clause, नमः अस्तु ते ‘homage be to you’ — the pattern of every refrain verse.
mantras.lit: O you who abide in the heart of every person in the form of understanding, giver of heaven and final release, O Goddess, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you.
mantras.tr: You dwell as understanding in the heart of every being, and you grant both heaven and final release: O Goddess Nārāyaṇī, salutation to you.
mantras.tr_note: The vocative epithets are turned into statements (‘You dwell …, you grant …’) and the address is gathered at the end.

comm.t: The first verse of the refrain. The Goddess is greeted as the understanding (buddhi) that lives in every heart, and as the giver of heaven and final release; the line नारायणि नमोऽस्तु ते, ‘O Nārāyaṇī, homage to you’, now closes every verse to 11.23.

The refrain gives the hymn its name, Nārāyaṇī Stuti. The thought of the first line repeats the yā devī stanza of chapter 5, या देवी सर्वभूतेषु बुद्धिरूपेण संस्थिता (5.20–22), and the second line returns at the end of the text, where the Goddess, worshipped, is भोगस्वर्गापवर्गदा (13.5).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has both names: स्वर्गापवर्गदा (764) and नारायणी (298), and also महाबुद्धिः (223). The agreement is in shared Śākta vocabulary; the two texts are separate works.

A modern reading: the Goddess is placed first not in heaven but in the mind’s power to understand. Clear understanding, on this view, is already her presence, and the way to both the good life and release runs through it.

As शक्ता with the locative it means ‘O you who are able to bring about the world’s dissolution’; as शक्ति, ‘O Power at work in the world’s dissolution’. The hymn calls her शक्ति in 11.5 and शक्तिभूते in 11.11, which favours शक्ति; the sense is close either way.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) कलाकाष्ठादिरूपेण परिणामप्रदायिनि, विश्वस्य उपरतौ शक्ते नारायणि, ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Vocatives (परिणामप्रदायिनि, शक्ते, नारायणि) followed by the refrain; the instrumental कलाकाष्ठादिरूपेण says how she brings change, the locative विश्वस्य उपरतौ where her power is shown.
mantras.lit: O you who, in the form of kalās, kāṣṭhās and the rest, bring about change; O Power in the dissolution of the universe, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you.
mantras.tr: As the moments and measures of time you bring all things through their changes, and yours is the power that brings the universe to rest: O Nārāyaṇī, salutation to you.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Moments and measures of time’ renders कला, काष्ठा and the rest, which are small units of time; ‘brings to rest’ renders उपरति ‘cessation’.

comm.t: The Goddess is time. As its units — kāṣṭhā, kalā and the rest — she brings every thing through its changes, and she is the power by which the universe at last comes to rest.

In the classical reckoning of time a kāṣṭhā is eighteen blinks (nimeṣa) and thirty kāṣṭhās make a kalā; the verse names the smallest measures to say that no moment is outside her. परिणाम, ‘transformation’, is the Sāṃkhya word for the change of prakṛti, and the text has already called her the supreme prakṛti (4.7, 1.78).
A modern reading: change and ending are named here among her gifts. The same power that sustains things also lets them pass, and both are met with salutation.

samasa.alt: Also read with a superlative sense, ‘the most auspicious among all auspicious things’; a partitive (‘among’) relation is expressed by the locative, सर्वमङ्गलेषु मङ्गल्या, a saptamī tatpuruṣa. The source-sense fits the verse’s run of epithets of blessing.

samasa.vigraha: सर्वे अर्थाः सर्वार्थाः; सर्वार्थान् साधयति इति सर्वार्थसाधिका, तत्सम्बुद्धौ
samasa.type: upapada tatpuruṣa (-साधिका, agent noun of the causative of √साध्) containing a karmadhāraya (सर्वार्थ)
samasa.sense: she who brings every purpose of her devotees to fulfilment

samasa.vigraha: त्रीणि अम्बकानि यस्याः सा त्र्यम्बका, तत्सम्बुद्धौ
samasa.sense: the three-eyed one, the consort of Tryambaka (Śiva)
samasa.alt: अम्बक is ‘eye’; the name is sometimes also connected with अम्बा ‘mother’, but the grammar of the word supports ‘three-eyed’.

morph.note: मङ्गल्य is a taddhita adjective from मङ्गल with -ya, ‘auspicious, bringing good fortune’; feminine मङ्गल्या, vocative -ल्ये. The variant माङ्गल्य (with vṛddhi) is the abstract noun ‘auspiciousness’ — see the flags.
साधक ‘one who accomplishes’ (causative of √साध् with -aka); in the feminine the a before k becomes i: साधिका.
Vocative of गौरी (‘the fair one’, the name of Pārvatī): the final ī is shortened in address.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) सर्वमङ्गलमङ्गल्ये शिवे सर्वार्थसाधिके शरण्ये त्र्यम्बके गौरि नारायणि, ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Seven vocatives in a row, then the refrain नमः अस्तु ते.
mantras.lit: O auspiciousness of all that is auspicious, O Śivā, accomplisher of every aim, O refuge, O three-eyed one, O Gaurī, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you.
mantras.tr: Blessing of all that is blessed, auspicious Śivā, who bring every aim to fulfilment, our refuge, three-eyed Gaurī: O Nārāyaṇī, salutation to you.
mantras.tr_note: शिवे is rendered both by its meaning ‘auspicious’ and as the name Śivā; the vocatives are grouped into phrases.

comm.t: A verse made only of names. She is the blessing in all that is blessed, Śivā, the one who fulfils every aim, the refuge, the three-eyed Gaurī — and, in the refrain, Nārāyaṇī.

This is the most widely recited verse of the Devī Māhātmya; it is said on its own as a verse of blessing at the beginning and end of worship and on auspicious occasions. Its names belong to Śiva’s consort (Śivā, Tryambakā, Gaurī), while the refrain names her as Nārāyaṇī, the power of Viṣṇu. The tradition reads this as the text’s teaching that the powers of all the gods are one Goddess (as in her birth from the gods’ combined radiance in chapter 2).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has सर्वमङ्गला (200), शिवा (53), त्र्यम्बका (762), गौरी (635) and नारायणी (298). Most names of this verse are among its names; the two texts are separate works.
A modern reading: a verse of pure address, asking nothing. It is recited at beginnings and endings because it names the good before any request is made.

flags.uncertain: Variant (corrections.json, status ‘Textual Verification Required’): GRETIL and Freund read सर्वमङ्गलमाङ्गल्ये, with the vṛddhi form माङ्गल्य (‘auspiciousness’). The Gita Press सर्वमङ्गलमङ्गल्ये, the form generally recited, is kept. The metre is unaffected (both are eight syllables, with the sixth heavy either way), and the sense — she is the auspiciousness of all auspicious things — is the same.

samasa.vigraha: सृष्टिः च स्थितिः च विनाशः च सृष्टिस्थितिविनाशाः, तेषाम्
samasa.sense: of the three acts of the world: its making, its keeping and its ending
samasa.alt: The compound takes the gender of its last member (विनाश, m.) and the plural for three members.

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (भूत ‘being, existing as’, as in आधारभूता, 11.4)
samasa.sense: you who are the very power behind creation, preservation and dissolution

samasa.vigraha: गुणानाम् आश्रयः यस्यां सा गुणाश्रया, तत्सम्बुद्धौ
samasa.literal: she in whom the guṇas have their resting-place
samasa.sense: the ground on which the three guṇas — sattva, rajas, tamas — rest
samasa.alt: Often translated as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, गुणानाम् आश्रयः ‘support of the guṇas’; but a tatpuruṣa keeps the gender of आश्रय (m.), and the feminine vocative -आश्रये shows the bahuvrīhi. The meaning is the same.

morph.note: -मय (mayaṭ) means ‘made of, consisting of’; its feminine is -मयी (vocative -मये). गुणाश्रये and गुणमये together say that she both supports the guṇas and is made of them.
सनातन ‘eternal’ (from सना ‘always’) with feminine -ī; vocative with the ī shortened.
Genitive plural of an a-stem dvandva: -आनाम्. It depends on the first member of the next word (शक्ति-), a construction common in verse.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) सृष्टिस्थितिविनाशानां शक्तिभूते सनातनि गुणाश्रये गुणमये नारायणि, ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Vocatives (शक्तिभूते, सनातनि, गुणाश्रये, गुणमये, नारायणि) followed by the refrain; the genitive dvandva depends on शक्ति-.
mantras.lit: O you who are the power of creation, preservation and destruction, O eternal one, O resting-place of the guṇas, O you who consist of the guṇas, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you.
mantras.tr: Eternal one, you are the power that creates, sustains and destroys; the guṇas rest in you and are made of you: O Nārāyaṇī, salutation to you.
mantras.tr_note: The vocative epithets are turned into statements. ‘Are made of you’ renders गुणमये (‘consisting of the guṇas’) from the other side; a closer rendering is ‘you are made of the guṇas’.

comm.t: The Goddess is the single power behind the three acts of the world — creation, continuance and destruction — and the eternal ground of the three guṇas, which both rest in her and make up her form.

The verse gathers the teaching of Brahmā’s hymn: in creation she is creation, in preserving she is preservation, at the end she is dissolution (1.76–77), and she is the prakṛti that brings forth the three guṇas (1.78, गुणत्रयविभाविनी). The tradition links the three acts with the three guṇas (rajas, sattva, tamas) and with Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra, all of whom act through her power. The word सनातनी returns in 12.39.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has सृष्टिकर्त्री (264), संहारिणी (268), त्रिगुणात्मिका (763) and also गुणातीता (961), ‘beyond the guṇas’. The two texts are separate works; together the names show the Śākta view that she is both within and beyond the guṇas.

samasa.vigraha: शरणम् आगताः शरणागताः; दीनाः च ते आर्ताः च दीनार्ताः; शरणागताः दीनार्ताः शरणागतदीनार्ताः; तेषां परित्राणम्; तत् परम् अयनं यस्याः सा शरणागतदीनार्तपरित्राणपरायणा, तत्सम्बुद्धौ
samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (-परायण ‘having … as highest goal’), containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (…परित्राण), a karmadhāraya (शरणागतदीनार्त), a dvitīyā tatpuruṣa (शरणागत) and a dvandva or karmadhāraya (दीनार्त)
samasa.literal: she whose highest aim is the rescue of the wretched and afflicted who have come for refuge
samasa.sense: she who lives to save the helpless who turn to her
samasa.alt: शरणागतदीनार्त can also be a three-member dvandva, ‘those who have taken refuge, the wretched and the afflicted’ (three groups instead of one). The karmadhāraya, one group described three ways, is the more common reading; the sense differs little.

samasa.sense: as in 11.3 (प्रपन्नार्तिहरे); the genitive सर्वस्य outside the compound depends on its first member आर्ति

morph.note: A single compound fills the whole first line (eight syllables). परायण at the end of a compound means ‘wholly devoted to, intent on’ (lit. ‘having … as the highest resort’). परित्राण is the action noun of परि + √त्रै ‘to rescue’.
-हर is the agent of √हृ ‘to take away’ in compounds, feminine -हरा; vocative -हरे.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) शरणागतदीनार्तपरित्राणपरायणे, सर्वस्य आर्तिहरे देवि नारायणि, ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two vocative phrases and the refrain; the first line is a single compound.
mantras.lit: O you who are wholly intent on rescuing the wretched and afflicted who have come for refuge, O Goddess who take away the distress of all, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you.
mantras.tr: You live to rescue the helpless and suffering who come to you for shelter, and you take away the sorrow of all: O Goddess Nārāyaṇī, salutation to you.
mantras.tr_note: The vocatives are turned into statements; ‘live to rescue’ renders -परायणे, ‘wholly intent on’.

comm.t: The Goddess is greeted as the one whose whole purpose is to rescue those who come to her in helplessness and pain, and who takes away the distress of all.

The verse returns to the first word of the hymn: प्रपन्नार्तिहरे (11.3) becomes सर्वस्यार्तिहरे, and the prapanna, the one who has come for refuge, becomes the शरणागत. The tradition values the verse as a prayer of surrender: it asks for nothing but names her as the refuge of the helpless.
A modern reading: the verse does not ask the one who comes for refuge to be worthy, only to be in need and to come. Refuge is described from the side of the one who gives it.

samasa.vigraha: हंसैः युक्तम् हंसयुक्तम्; हंसयुक्तं च तत् विमानं च हंसयुक्तविमानम्; हंसयुक्तविमाने तिष्ठति इति हंसयुक्तविमानस्था, तत्सम्बुद्धौ

samasa.literal: she who stands in the car yoked with swans
samasa.sense: Brahmāṇī, riding the swan-drawn chariot of Brahmā

samasa.vigraha: ब्रह्माण्याः रूपम् ब्रह्माणीरूपम्; तत् धारयति इति ब्रह्माणीरूपधारिणी, तत्सम्बुद्धौ

samasa.literal: bearer of the form of Brahmāṇī
samasa.sense: you who take the form of Brahmā’s Śakti

samasa.vigraha: कौशम् अम्भः कौशाम्भः; तत् क्षरयति इति कौशाम्भःक्षरिका, तत्सम्बुद्धौ
samasa.sense: you who sprinkle water consecrated with kuśa grass

morph.note: कौश is a taddhita from कुश (with vṛddhi): ‘of kuśa grass’, i.e. water sprinkled with or sanctified by kuśa. क्षरिका is an agent noun from √क्षर् ‘to flow’ (here ‘to make flow, sprinkle’) with the suffix -aka, feminine -ikā; the formation is uncommon, and the word is known chiefly from this verse.
ब्रह्माणी is the feminine of ब्रह्मन् formed with -ānī (like इन्द्राणी, रुद्राणी): Brahmā’s consort or power. -धारिन् (√धृ with -in) ‘bearing’, feminine -धारिणी.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) हंसयुक्तविमानस्थे ब्रह्माणीरूपधारिणि कौशाम्भःक्षरिके देवि नारायणि, ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three descriptive vocatives naming Brahmāṇī, then देवि नारायणि and the refrain.
mantras.lit: O you who are seated in the celestial car yoked with swans, who bear the form of Brahmāṇī, who sprinkle water with kuśa grass, O Goddess, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you.
mantras.tr: Riding the swan-drawn chariot in the form of Brahmāṇī, sprinkling the water hallowed with kuśa grass: O Goddess Nārāyaṇī, salutation to you.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Hallowed with kuśa’ interprets कौश- (‘of kuśa’): in rites, water is sprinkled with a bunch of kuśa grass.

comm.t: With this verse the hymn turns to the Mātṛkās, the Śaktis of the gods who fought beside the Goddess against Raktabīja’s army (chapter 8): Brahmāṇī here, then Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Aindrī, Śivadūtī and Cāmuṇḍā (11.14–21). Each is greeted as a form of the one Nārāyaṇī.

The picture is the one given in the battle: Brahmāṇī came on a car drawn by swans, with rosary and water-pot (8.15), and struck down the asuras by sprinkling water from her kamaṇḍalu (8.33), water made pure by mantra (9.38). The hymn turns her weapon into an image of blessing: the sprinkling of consecrated water.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also has the name ब्रह्माणी (821). The Mātṛkās are a shared Śākta group; the two texts are separate works.

flags.uncertain: क्षरिका is a rare formation (from √क्षर् ‘to flow, let flow’); the sense ‘sprinkler of water’ is clear from the context and from 8.33, but the exact derivation is not certain.

samasa.literal: she who rides the great bull
samasa.sense: riding Nandin, Śiva’s bull
samasa.alt: Also analysed with the possessive suffix -in on वाह ‘mount’: ‘having the great bull as her mount’ (महावृषभः वाहः अस्याः अस्ति). The sense is the same.

samasa.sense: as Māheśvarī, the Śakti of Maheśvara (Śiva)

morph.note: An instrumental, not a vocative: the verse has no vocative ‘O Māheśvarī’ but says ‘(you who are) in the form of Māheśvarī’. The refrain’s नारायणि is the only name in the address.
-धर (√धृ with -a) ‘bearing, holding’, feminine -धरा; vocative -धरे.
महत् ‘great’ becomes महा at the head of a karmadhāraya (a rule of compound formation, not of sandhi), as in महासुर (11.2).

mantras.anvaya_en: Two vocatives, an instrumental of manner (with a participle such as स्थिते understood), and the refrain.
mantras.lit: O bearer of the trident, the moon and the serpent, O rider of the great bull, O Nārāyaṇī (who are) in the form of Māheśvarī, homage be to you.
mantras.tr: Bearing the trident, the crescent moon and the serpent, riding the great bull in the form of Māheśvarī: O Nārāyaṇī, salutation to you.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Crescent’ is added to ‘moon’ (चन्द्र), as Māheśvarī is described in 8.16 with the moon’s digit (चन्द्ररेखा).

comm.t: The second of the Mātṛkās: Māheśvarī, Śiva’s Śakti, with his emblems — the trident, the crescent moon and the serpent — and riding his great bull.

So she came to the battle in chapter 8: mounted on the bull, holding the trident, with great serpents for bracelets and the moon’s crescent as her ornament (8.16), and she slew asuras with her trident (8.34, 8.49). The hymn salutes the same figure as a form of Nārāyaṇī.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also has the name माहेश्वरी (208). The two texts are separate works.

samasa.vigraha: मयूराः च कुक्कुटाः च मयूरकुक्कुटाः; तैः वृता मयूरकुक्कुटवृता, तत्सम्बुद्धौ
samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa containing an itaretara dvandva
samasa.sense: attended by the birds of Skanda: the peacock his mount, the cock his banner

samasa.vigraha: महती चासौ शक्तिः च महाशक्तिः; तां धरति इति महाशक्तिधरा, तत्सम्बुद्धौ
samasa.sense: you who hold the great spear (शक्ति), Skanda’s weapon
samasa.alt: शक्ति means both ‘spear’ and ‘power’; ‘bearer of great power’ is possible, but Kaumārī’s weapon in the battle is the śakti-spear (8.17, शक्तिहस्ता), which fixes the first sense. The pun is natural in a hymn to the Śakti.

samasa.vigraha: न विद्यते अघं यस्याः सा अनघा, तत्सम्बुद्धौ
samasa.literal: she in whom there is no sin
samasa.sense: O spotless, faultless one

samasa.vigraha: कौमार्याः रूपम् कौमारीरूपम्; कौमारीरूपं संस्थानं यस्याः सा कौमारीरूपसंस्थाना, तत्सम्बुद्धौ
samasa.literal: she whose configuration is the form of Kaumārī
samasa.sense: you who appear as Kaumārī, the Śakti of Kumāra (Skanda)
samasa.alt: संस्थान can also be ‘abiding’: ‘she whose abiding is in Kaumārī’s form’ (कौमारीरूपे संस्थानं यस्याः). The sense is the same.

morph.note: वृत is the past participle of √वृ (svādi, ‘to cover, surround’): ‘surrounded, attended’; feminine -वृता, vocative -वृते.
कौमारी is a taddhita from कुमार (with vṛddhi and feminine -ī): ‘belonging to Kumāra’, i.e. Skanda’s Śakti.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) मयूरकुक्कुटवृते महाशक्तिधरे अनघे कौमारीरूपसंस्थाने नारायणि, ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Four vocative epithets of Kaumārī, then the refrain.
mantras.lit: O you who are attended by peacocks and cocks, bearer of the great spear, O sinless one, you whose shape is the form of Kaumārī, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you.
mantras.tr: Attended by peacock and cock, holding the mighty spear, spotless one in the form of Kaumārī: O Nārāyaṇī, salutation to you.

comm.t: The third Mātṛkā: Kaumārī, the Śakti of Kumāra (Skanda), with his birds, the peacock and the cock, and his great spear.

In the battle Kaumārī came spear in hand, riding a fine peacock, in the form of Guha (8.17), and slew asuras with her spear (8.34, 8.49; 9.38). The peacock is Skanda’s mount and the cock his banner in Purāṇic iconography.
A modern reading: अनघा, ‘sinless’, stands in the middle of a warrior’s description. The force that fights here is pictured as clean of malice.

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi containing an itaretara dvandva (शङ्खचक्रगदाशार्ङ्ग) and a karmadhāraya (परमायुध)
samasa.literal: she by whom the supreme weapons, conch, discus, mace and Śārṅga, have been taken up
samasa.sense: you who carry Viṣṇu’s weapons
samasa.alt: The participle गृहीत stands between the two groups. The compound may also be divided as शङ्खचक्रगदाशार्ङ्गगृहीता (‘who has taken conch … Śārṅga’, with the participle placed second, as is allowed in such bahuvrīhis) and परमायुधा (‘whose weapons are supreme’); the sense is the same.

samasa.vigraha: वैष्णव्याः रूपं यस्याः सा वैष्णवीरूपा, तत्सम्बुद्धौ
samasa.literal: she whose form is (that of) Vaiṣṇavī
samasa.sense: you who appear as Vaiṣṇavī, Viṣṇu’s Śakti

morph.note: गृहीत is the past participle of √ग्रह् (kryādi, ‘to seize’): the ra of the root becomes ṛ (samprasāraṇa) and the connecting vowel is long (गृह् + ई + त). शार्ङ्ग, Viṣṇu’s bow, is a taddhita from शृङ्ग ‘horn’: ‘made of horn’.
As in 11.3: the only imperative in the refrain verses so far besides अस्तु, a direct prayer inside the salutation.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) शङ्खचक्रगदाशार्ङ्गगृहीतपरमायुधे वैष्णवीरूपे नारायणि, प्रसीद; ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: A compound vocative fills the first line; the second adds a prayer (प्रसीद) to the refrain.
mantras.lit: O you who have taken up the supreme weapons — conch, discus, mace and Śārṅga — be gracious, O you in the form of Vaiṣṇavī, O Nārāyaṇī; homage be to you.
mantras.tr: Holding the conch, the discus, the mace and the bow Śārṅga, those supreme weapons, in the form of Vaiṣṇavī — be gracious, O Nārāyaṇī; salutation to you.

comm.t: The fourth Mātṛkā: Vaiṣṇavī, the Śakti of Viṣṇu, holding his four weapons — conch, discus, mace and the bow Śārṅga. In this verse alone of the Mātṛkā series the gods add a prayer, प्रसीद, ‘be gracious’.

In the battle Vaiṣṇavī came seated on Garuḍa, with conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow and sword in her hands (8.18), and her discus struck and pierced Raktabīja (8.47–48). Here the name of the refrain and the name of the form coincide: Nārāyaṇī is greeted as Vaiṣṇavī, the power of Nārāyaṇa himself (compare 11.5, वैष्णवी शक्तिः).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the names वैष्णवी (892) and विष्णुरूपिणी (893). The two texts are separate works.

mantras.anvaya_en: Four vocatives of Vārāhī, then the refrain.
mantras.lit: O you who have taken up the fierce great discus, who raised the earth with your tusk, O you who have the form of a boar, O auspicious one, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you.
mantras.tr: Wielding the fierce great discus, raising the earth upon your tusk, auspicious one in the form of the Boar: O Nārāyaṇī, salutation to you.

comm.t: The fifth Mātṛkā: Vārāhī, the Śakti of the Boar. She is greeted with the Boar’s great deed: lifting the earth on its tusk.

In the battle the Śakti of Hari, who bears the form of the sacrificial Boar, came in a boar’s body (8.19) and fought beside the others (8.49; 9.39, where her snout crushes asuras). The hymn gives her the Boar’s own deed, the raising of the earth from the waters, so that the deed of Viṣṇu’s avatāra is praised as hers.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also knows Vārāhī as a warrior power: name 76, विशुक्रप्राणहरणवाराहीवीर्यनन्दिता, ‘delighted by the valour of Vārāhī, who took Viśukra’s life’. The battles are different and the two texts are separate works.

morph.note: Infinitive of purpose (√हन् + tum): ‘in order to slay’, depending on कृतोद्यमे.
त्रैलोक्य is a taddhita (with vṛddhi) from त्रिलोक ‘the three worlds’: ‘the triad of worlds’. सहित ‘accompanied by, joined with’ (सह + हित) here means ‘devoted to’.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) उग्रेण नृसिंहरूपेण दैत्यान् हन्तुं कृतोद्यमे, त्रैलोक्यत्राणसहिते नारायणि, ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is one vocative phrase built on कृतोद्यमे, with an instrumental of manner and an infinitive of purpose; the second adds a further vocative and the refrain.
mantras.lit: O you who, in the fierce form of the Man-Lion, set out with resolve to slay the Daityas, O you who are bent on protecting the three worlds, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you.
mantras.tr: In the terrible form of the Man-Lion you rose to slay the demons, intent on saving the three worlds: O Nārāyaṇī, salutation to you.
mantras.tr_note: The vocatives are turned into statements.

comm.t: The sixth Mātṛkā: Nārasiṃhī, the Śakti of the Man-Lion, in her fierce form, set on destroying the Daityas to protect the three worlds.

In the battle Nārasiṃhī came in a body like Nṛsiṃha’s, scattering the stars with the toss of her mane (8.20), and roamed the field tearing asuras with her claws (8.37). As in 11.17, the purpose of Viṣṇu’s avatāra — to protect the worlds from the Daityas — is praised as the Goddess’s own.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has a related idea in name 80, कराङ्गुलिनखोत्पन्ननारायणदशाकृतिः, ‘from whose fingernails arose the ten forms of Nārāyaṇa’: there too Viṣṇu’s avatāras, the Boar and the Man-Lion among them, come from the Goddess. The two texts are separate works.

mantras.anvaya: हे किरीटिनि महावज्रे सहस्रनयनोज्ज्वले वृत्रप्राणहरे च ऐन्द्रि नारायणि, ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: A chain of vocatives ending in the name ऐन्द्रि; च adds the last epithet. The refrain नारायणि नमोऽस्तु ते is the main clause.
mantras.lit: O crowned one, O you of the great thunderbolt, O you who blaze with a thousand eyes, and O Aindrī, taker of Vṛtra’s life — O Nārāyaṇī, let homage be to you.
mantras.tr: Crowned, wielding the great thunderbolt, ablaze with a thousand eyes, Aindrī who took the life of Vṛtra — Nārāyaṇī, salutation to you.

comm.t: The seventh of the Mātṛkā stanzas (11.13–21). The Goddess is praised as Aindrī, Indra’s power, as she came to the battlefield in 8.21 (वज्रहस्ता … गजराजोपरि स्थिता … सहस्रनयना यथा शक्रः) and struck Raktabīja with her thunderbolt (8.42, 8.46). Every attribute is Indra’s: the diadem, the vajra, the thousand eyes, the killing of Vṛtra.

In 8.13–14 the powers of the gods leave their bodies with the same form, ornaments and mounts as the gods themselves. The hymn names each Mātṛkā by her god’s deed: Vārāhī lifts the earth on her tusk (11.17), Nārasiṃhī strikes the daityas (11.18), Aindrī slays Vṛtra. The Vedic victory of Indra is credited to the power through which he won it.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name वज्रिणी (name 944), ‘she who holds the thunderbolt’. The image is shared; the two texts are separate works.

samasa.sense: destroyer of the asura host (9.23, 9.37, 9.41)
samasa.alt: बल can also mean ‘strength’: हताः दैत्याः यया सा च महाबला च, ‘slayer of the daityas, of great might’. The compound is printed as one word, and बल ‘army’ with हत ‘slain’ reads more naturally; both senses fit the narrative.

samasa.sense: fearsome to behold (8.23 अतिभीषणा … अत्युग्रा)
the howl of a hundred jackals (8.23 शिवाशतनिनादिनी) and her laughter (9.23)

morph.note: Instrumental of manner among vocatives, as माहेश्वरीस्वरूपेण in 11.14: ‘(you who appear) in the form of Śivadūtī’.
हत is the past participle (kta) of √हन् (adādi 2P ‘to strike, kill’); as the first member of a bahuvrīhi it gives the passive sense ‘by whom … was slain’.

mantras.anvaya: हे शिवदूतीस्वरूपेण (स्थिते) हतदैत्यमहाबले घोररूपे महारावे नारायणि, ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: The instrumental phrase describes the manner of her appearance; three bahuvrīhi vocatives follow; then the refrain.
mantras.lit: (You who are) in the form of Śivadūtī, O you by whom the great army of the daityas was slain, O you of terrible form, O you of the mighty roar — O Nārāyaṇī, let homage be to you.
mantras.tr: Appearing as Śivadūtī, destroyer of the daityas’ mighty host, terrible of form, loud of roar — Nārāyaṇī, salutation to you.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Appearing’ supplies the participle implied by the instrumental of form.

comm.t: The eighth Mātṛkā stanza praises Śivadūtī, the fierce power that sprang from Caṇḍikā’s own body, howling like a hundred jackals (8.23). She sent Śiva as her envoy to Śumbha and Niśumbha (8.24–27) and so was named Śivadūtī, ‘she who has Śiva as messenger’ (8.28). Her laughter terrified the asuras (8.38, 9.23) and she devoured them (9.37, 9.41).

Unlike the six Mātṛkās before her, Śivadūtī is no god’s power but the Devī’s own: she comes from Caṇḍikā’s body, not from a god’s. The stanza thus moves from the gods’ śaktis back to the Goddess herself, completed by Cāmuṇḍā in 11.21.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name शिवदूती (name 405). The name and its sense are shared Śākta usage; the two texts are separate works.

samasa.type: upapada tatpuruṣa (मथन = √मथ् with the agent affix -अन)
samasa.sense: slayer of the general Muṇḍa (7.21)
samasa.alt: Also a bahuvrīhi: मुण्डस्य मथनं यया सा, ‘she by whom the crushing of Muṇḍa (was done)’; or with मुण्ड in its common-noun sense ‘shaven head’, ‘crusher of heads’. The proper name fits the pairing with चामुण्डे.

morph.note: Vocative of चामुण्डा. The text gives the name’s origin in 7.27: because Kālī brought the heads of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, she would be known as Cāmuṇḍā (यस्माच्चण्डं च मुण्डं च … चामुण्डेति ततो लोके ख्याता देवि भविष्यसि). It is a name, not a regular compound.
मथन is an agent noun from √मथ् / मन्थ् (‘to churn, crush’) in -अन; feminine मथना, vocative मथने.

mantras.anvaya: हे दंष्ट्राकरालवदने शिरोमालाविभूषणे मुण्डमथने चामुण्डे नारायणि, ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two bahuvrīhi vocatives describing her appearance, the name with its explanatory epithet, then the refrain.
mantras.lit: O you whose face is dreadful with tusks, O you whose ornament is a garland of heads, O Cāmuṇḍā, O crusher of Muṇḍa — O Nārāyaṇī, let homage be to you.
mantras.tr: Fanged and fearful of face, garlanded with heads, Cāmuṇḍā, slayer of Muṇḍa — Nārāyaṇī, salutation to you.

comm.t: The last Mātṛkā stanza praises Cāmuṇḍā, the Kālī who sprang from Ambikā’s brow (7.5–7), killed Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (7.20–21) and received her name for it (7.27). In the Raktabīja battle she drank the demon’s blood so that no new asura could rise from it (8.53–61). The epithets are those of her first appearance: a gaping fanged mouth and a garland of heads.

With Cāmuṇḍā the series of nine forms (Brahmāṇī to Cāmuṇḍā, 11.13–21) is complete. In the Śākta tradition these forms are worshipped as the Mātṛkās, the ‘Mothers’, with Cāmuṇḍā often counted among them; the hymn presents them all as forms of one Nārāyaṇī.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names her चण्डमुण्डासुरनिषूदिनी (name 756), ‘destroyer of the asuras Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa’ — the same story in a different text.

The two vocatives are printed without a space; nothing changes at the junction.

samasa.sense: the supreme knowledge that frees (cf. 1.57 सा विद्या परमा मुक्तेर्हेतुभूता)
the night of dissolution, as in Brahmā’s hymn (1.79 कालरात्रिर्महारात्रिर्मोहरात्रिश्च दारुणा)

samasa.vigraha: महती अविद्या (महाविद्या), तत्सम्बुद्धौ; अविद्या = न विद्या
samasa.sense: the ignorance that binds, also her power (cf. 1.58 संसारबन्धहेतुश्च सैव)
samasa.alt: Without the avagraha (GRETIL, Freund) the word is महाविद्ये again, ‘great knowledge’, repeating the first line. The Gita Press reading pairs it with महारात्रि and balances महाविद्ये in the first line.

morph.note: लक्ष्मी is an ī-stem of the type that keeps visarga in the nominative (लक्ष्मीः); the vocative shortens the ī: लक्ष्मि. Contrast the ā-stems of the line, whose vocative ends in -e (लज्जे, श्रद्धे, स्वधे).

The i-stem vocative should be पुष्टे (guṇa of the final). The printed पुष्टि (written together with स्वधे) keeps the stem form, as भूति does in 11.23; Purāṇic verse allows such vocatives. The metre is unaffected.
रात्रि has a by-form रात्री (ī-stem); the vocative of महारात्री is महारात्रि. (Of the i-stem, used in 1.79, it would be महारात्रे.)

mantras.anvaya: हे लक्ष्मि लज्जे महाविद्ये श्रद्धे पुष्टि स्वधे ध्रुवे महारात्रि महाऽविद्ये नारायणि, ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Nine names in the vocative, each a power the Goddess is; then the refrain.
mantras.lit: O Lakṣmī, O Modesty, O Great Knowledge, O Faith, O Nourishment, O Svadhā, O Steadfast One, O Great Night, O Great Nescience — O Nārāyaṇī, let homage be to you.
mantras.tr: Fortune, Modesty, Great Knowledge, Faith, Nourishment, Svadhā, the Steadfast; Great Night and Great Ignorance — Nārāyaṇī, salutation to you.

comm.t: After the nine warrior forms the hymn turns to abstract powers. Most of these names were already given her by Brahmā (1.73 स्वधा, 1.77 महाविद्या, 1.79 महारात्रिः, 1.80 लज्जा पुष्टिः) and by the gods (4.5 श्रीः … श्रद्धा … लज्जा; 5.44–58 लज्जा, श्रद्धा, लक्ष्मी).

The line ends on a pair of opposites: महाविद्या ‘great knowledge’ at the start of the first line, महाऽविद्या ‘great nescience’ at the end of the second. The Gita Press marks the second with an avagraha; other witnesses (GRETIL, Freund) read महाविद्ये twice. Both readings are traditional (corrections.json, variant).

The Gita Press reading states a teaching the text gives from the start: the same Mahāmāyā is the knowledge that liberates and the power that binds (1.57–58 सा विद्या परमा मुक्तेर्हेतुभूता … संसारबन्धहेतुश्च सैव). Knowledge and ignorance are not two goddesses.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has महाविद्या (name 584) and विद्याऽविद्यास्वरूपिणी (name 402), ‘whose form is both knowledge and ignorance’, and also लज्जा (740), पुष्टिः (444) and स्वधा (536). The pairing of knowledge and nescience is a shared Śākta idea; the texts are separate works.

flags.uncertain: Variant (recorded): महाऽविद्ये (Gita Press, kept) against महाविद्ये (GRETIL, Freund) — two readings, ‘great nescience’ or ‘great knowledge’; both traditional. The digital text prints पुष्टिस्वधे as one word; it is taken here as two vocatives (पुष्टि, a stem-form vocative for पुष्टे, and स्वधे), since a dvandva of two names would not stand in the vocative singular. If the joining is deliberate, the alternative is an irregular compound vocative of ‘Puṣṭi-Svadhā’.

morph.note: The i-stem vocative would be भूते. The text has भूति, a stem-form vocative found in Purāṇic verse (compare पुष्टि in 11.22). The syllable count is the same either way.

Taken as the regular vocative of नियति (नि + √यम्, kṛt -ति) ‘restraint, fixed order, destiny’, which fits a list of powers (मेधा, भूति). It can also be the vocative of नियता (kta of नि + √यम्) ‘self-restrained one’; the form is the same.
Imperative of प्र + √सद्: the root takes the present stem सीद- (सद् → सीद), and with प्र means ‘be pleased, be gracious’.
Taddhita: तमस् + अ with vṛddhi (त → ता) gives तामस ‘belonging to tamas’; feminine तामसी, vocative तामसि.

mantras.anvaya: हे मेधे सरस्वति वरे भूति बाभ्रवि तामसि नियते ईशे, त्वं प्रसीद। (हे) नारायणि, ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Seven vocatives, a prayer (त्वं प्रसीद) with an eighth vocative (ईशे) set inside it, then the refrain.
mantras.lit: O Medhā, O Sarasvatī, O excellent one, O Prosperity, O Bābhravī, O Tāmasī, O Niyati — you, be gracious, O sovereign Lady; O Nārāyaṇī, let homage be to you.
mantras.tr: Intelligence, Sarasvatī, most excellent, Prosperity, tawny Bābhravī, dark Tāmasī, Ordaining Power — be gracious, sovereign Lady. Nārāyaṇī, salutation to you.
mantras.tr_note: बाभ्रवि and तामसि are rendered with their literal sense (‘tawny’, ‘dark’) as well as the name.

comm.t: The list of powers continues: intellect and speech (मेधा, सरस्वती), prosperity (भूति), and two names of her darker nature (बाभ्रवी, तामसी), closing with Niyati, the power that fixes the order of things. In the middle of the list the gods break into a direct prayer: त्वं प्रसीद, ‘be gracious’.

Medhā and Sarasvatī recall the gods’ hymn of chapter 4 (4.11 मेधासि देवि विदिताखिलशास्त्रसारा). Tāmasī is the Goddess as tamas, the power of sleep and dissolution: Brahmā’s hymn calls her the bearer of the three guṇas (1.78 गुणत्रयविभाविनी), and in the first carita she is Viṣṇu’s yoganidrā, his sleep (1.66, 1.69–71).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also has मेधा (name 538) and सरस्वती (name 704). Shared names; separate works.

flags.uncertain: भूति (and पुष्टि in 11.22) are stem-form vocatives, not the regular भूते; kept as printed. नियते may be read as Niyati ‘destiny’ (chosen) or नियता ‘the self-restrained’. बाभ्रवी: lexically ‘tawny’ (from बभ्रु) or ‘belonging to Babhru’; the specific mythological reference is not stated in the text.

mantras.anvaya: हे सर्वस्वरूपे सर्वेशे सर्वशक्तिसमन्विते देवि, नः भयेभ्यः त्राहि। हे दुर्गे देवि, ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three bahuvrīhi and tatpuruṣa vocatives, then a prayer (त्राहि नः) and a new refrain addressed to Durgā.
mantras.lit: O you whose form is all, O Lady of all, O you endowed with every power — protect us from fears, O Devī; O Durgā, O Devī, let homage be to you.
mantras.tr: Form of all things, Lady of all, possessed of every power — protect us from every fear, Devī. Durgā, Devī, salutation to you.
mantras.tr_note: ‘every fear’ renders the plural भयेभ्यः.

comm.t: The refrain changes. After sixteen stanzas ending नारायणि नमोऽस्तु ते (11.8–23), the gods address her as Durgā and ask for protection from fear. From here to 11.28 each stanza is a prayer for protection, as at the end of the gods’ hymn in chapter 4 (4.24–27 शूलेन पाहि नो देवि …).

The name Durgā is explained later in this chapter: the Devī foretells that she will slay the asura Durgama and be known as Durgā Devī (11.49–50). Traditionally this stanza is among the most widely recited of the Saptaśatī, used on its own as a prayer for freedom from fear.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has दुर्गा (name 190), सर्वेश्वरी (name 202), सर्वशक्तिमयी (name 199) and भयापहा (name 121), ‘remover of fear’. Shared names and ideas; the works are separate.

mantras.anvaya_en: The subject (वदनम् with three qualifiers) and the imperative पातु; then the refrain to Kātyāyanī.
mantras.lit: May this gentle face of yours, adorned with three eyes, protect us from all fears; O Kātyāyanī, let homage be to you.
mantras.tr: May this gentle face of yours, graced with three eyes, protect us from every fear. Kātyāyanī, salutation to you.

comm.t: The first of four stanzas (11.25–28) in which the Goddess’s own attributes — her face, trident, bell and sword — are asked to protect. The gods began this hymn by praising her as Kātyāyanī (11.2 कात्यायनीं तुष्टुवुः), and the asuras sought her under that name (8.29 यत्र कात्यायनी स्थिता).

The gentle face is asked first, the fierce weapons after. The gods of chapter 4 prayed in the same order of thought: ‘protect us with your gentle forms and with your terrible ones’ (4.26 सौम्यानि यानि रूपाणि … यानि चात्यर्थघोराणि तै रक्षास्मान्).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has कात्यायनी (name 556) and त्र्यम्बका (name 762), ‘the three-eyed’. Shared names; separate works.

mantras.anvaya: हे भद्रकालि, ज्वालाकरालम् अत्युग्रम् अशेषासुरसूदनं (ते) त्रिशूलं नः भीतेः पातु। ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is three qualifiers of त्रिशूलम्, the subject of पातु; then the refrain to Bhadrakālī.
mantras.lit: May the trident — dreadful with flames, exceedingly fierce, destroyer of the asuras without remainder — protect us from fear; O Bhadrakālī, let homage be to you.
mantras.tr: May your trident, fearsome with flames, fiercer than fierce, slayer of every asura, protect us from fear. Bhadrakālī, salutation to you.
mantras.tr_note: ‘your’ is supplied from the context of the series (ते in 11.25 and 11.28).

comm.t: The trident is asked to protect. It is Māheśvarī’s weapon (11.14 त्रिशूलचन्द्राहिधरे; 8.49 माहेश्वरी त्रिशूलेन) and the first weapon named in the gods’ prayer of chapter 4 (4.24 शूलेन पाहि नो देवि). The name Bhadrakālī closed the account of the second carita’s hymn (4.39 तथेत्युक्त्वा भद्रकाली बभूवान्तर्हिता नृप).

The name joins two opposites: भद्र, ‘auspicious’, and काली, ‘the dark one’. The weapon that destroyed every asura is the protection of those who take refuge in her; the fierce form is fearsome only to what is hostile.
A modern reading: the prayer is not ‘protect us from enemies’ but ‘protect us from fear’ (भीतेः). The danger named is the inner state as much as the outer threat.

morph.note: √हिंस् is a rudhādi (seventh-class) root: the strong present inserts न before the final consonant, and the root’s own nasal falls away: हि-न-स्-ति (pl. हिंसन्ति).
Absolutive of the prefixed causative-type stem आ-पूरय-: with a prefix the absolutive takes -य (ल्यप्) and the stem’s -अय- is dropped: आपूर्य ‘having filled’.
Neuter s-stem plural: तेजस् → तेजांसि, with lengthened vowel and the nasal before s (as मनांसि, यशांसि).

The enclitic नः occurs twice. The first is the object of पातु (‘protect us’); the second is taken as genitive with पापेभ्यः (‘from our sins’). It may also be the object repeated for emphasis; the sense hardly changes.

mantras.anvaya: हे देवि, या (घण्टा) स्वनेन जगत् आपूर्य दैत्यतेजांसि हिनस्ति, सा घण्टा नः पापेभ्यः नः पातु, सुतान् इव।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (या … हिनस्ति, with the absolutive phrase स्वनेन जगत् आपूर्य) describes the bell; the main clause is सा घण्टा … पातु; सुतान् इव is a comparison.
mantras.lit: Which, having filled the world with its sound, destroys the fiery strength of the daityas — may that bell, O Devī, protect us from our sins, as children.
mantras.tr: Your bell, whose sound fills the world and breaks the daityas’ strength — may that bell, Devī, guard us from our sins, as children are guarded.
mantras.tr_note: ‘as children are guarded’ renders सुतान् इव; the Sanskrit does not name who guards them. ‘Your’ is supplied from the series.

comm.t: The bell is asked to protect. In the battle the Devī’s bell swelled the lion’s roar (8.9 घण्टास्वनेन तन्नादमम्बिका चोपबृंहयत्), and in the fight with Śumbha she filled the quarters with its sound, ‘which destroyed the strength of all the daitya armies’ (9.20 निजघण्टास्वनेन … समस्तदैत्यसैन्यानां तेजोवधविधायिना). The stanza recalls that line almost word for word (हिनस्ति दैत्यतेजांसि).

The sound that undid the demons’ strength is now asked to guard against sins: the outer enemy of the narrative becomes the inner enemy of the worshipper. The gods asked the same in chapter 4 (4.24 घण्टास्वनेन नः पाहि). A bell is rung in the rite of worship, and the hymn gives that sound a protective sense.
A modern reading: ‘as children’ makes the protection parental, not military — the same power that terrifies the hostile is tender toward its own.

flags.uncertain: The Gita Press prints पापेभ्योऽनः with an avagraha (also in its appendix); grammar has पापेभ्यः + नः, and no letter is elided. The avagraha is kept as printed and recorded as an orthographic variant (corrections.json); the witnesses read पापेभ्यो नः. The missing space after देवि in the digital text has been corrected.

mantras.anvaya: हे चण्डिके, असुरासृग्वसापङ्कचर्चितः करोज्ज्वलः ते खड्गः (नः) शुभाय भवतु। वयं त्वां नताः (स्मः)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A benediction (खड्गः … शुभाय भवतु) with two qualifiers of the sword, and a closing statement (वयं त्वां नताः) in place of the refrain.
mantras.lit: Smeared with the mire of the asuras’ blood and fat, gleaming in your hand — may your sword be for (our) good, O Caṇḍikā; we are bowed to you.
mantras.tr: Your sword, flashing in your hand and smeared with the blood and fat of the asuras — may it be for our good, Caṇḍikā. We bow to you.
mantras.tr_note: ‘our’ is supplied: शुभाय names no one.

comm.t: The last of the protection stanzas asks the sword to be ‘for good’. It is the weapon with which the Devī cut down Muṇḍa (7.21) and beheaded Niśumbha (9.33, 9.36), and which the gods named among her weapons in 4.27 (खड्गशूलगदादीनि … तैरस्मान् रक्ष सर्वतः). The refrain becomes a plain statement: ‘we are bowed to you’.

A sword still wet with blood is asked for auspiciousness. The gods of chapter 4 already saw the paradox: her weapons purify even the enemies they strike, who go to the higher worlds (4.18–19 लोकान् प्रयान्तु रिपवोऽपि हि शस्त्रपूता). The violence is directed at what threatens the world.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has चण्डिका (name 755). The name is shared; the works are separate.

samasa.sense: all, every one

morph.note: Present second singular of अप + √हन्: हन् + सि → हंसि, the n becoming anusvāra before s inside the word. With अप ‘away’: ‘you strike away, remove’. It governs both lines: रोगान् … अपहंसि, and (अपहंसि) कामान्.
Past participles of intransitive roots used in the active sense, with the force of a conditional: तुष्टा ‘(you,) when pleased’, रुष्टा ‘when angry’.
Abstract noun in -ता on आश्रय ‘refuge’: ‘refuge-hood’. With प्रयान्ति: ‘they attain the state of being a refuge’, i.e. they become a shelter for others.
विपद् is a root noun (वि + √पद् ‘to fall apart’) with no visible affix; its final d is pronounced t at a pause, so the padaccheda gives विपत्.

mantras.anvaya: (हे देवि, त्वं) तुष्टा (सती) अशेषान् रोगान् अपहंसि, रुष्टा तु सकलान् अभीष्टान् कामान् (अपहंसि)। त्वाम् आश्रितानां नराणां विपत् न (भवति)। त्वाम् आश्रिताः हि आश्रयतां प्रयान्ति।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two balanced clauses with one verb (अपहंसि), conditioned by तुष्टा and रुष्टा; then two statements about those who take refuge in her.
mantras.lit: Pleased, you strike away diseases without remainder; but angered, all longed-for desires. For men who have taken refuge in you there is no calamity; those who have taken refuge in you indeed attain the state of being a refuge.
mantras.tr: Pleased, you take away every illness; angered, every cherished hope. No misfortune befalls those who take refuge in you; those who take refuge in you become a refuge themselves.
mantras.tr_note: ‘become a refuge’ renders आश्रयतां प्रयान्ति ‘attain refuge-hood’.

comm.t: The hymn returns to the long metre of its opening stanzas (11.2–6; here indravajrā, eleven syllables a line). The first half sets out her power over fortune: her pleasure removes disease, her anger removes everything one longs for. The second half states the reward of refuge: no calamity, and more — the one who takes refuge becomes a refuge.

Traditionally this stanza is recited on its own as a prayer for freedom from illness. The last line is read as the fruit of devotion: the devotee’s protection reaches beyond himself to those who in turn depend on him.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) calls her भवरोगघ्नी (name 842), ‘destroyer of the disease of worldly existence’, and रोगपर्वतदम्भोलिः (name 748), ‘a thunderbolt to the mountain of disease’. The idea is shared; the works are separate.
A modern reading: refuge is not only received but passed on. Those who are held become able to hold others.

mantras.anvaya: हे देवि अम्बिके, अनेकैः रूपैः आत्ममूर्तिं बहुधा कृत्वा त्वया अद्य धर्मद्विषां महासुराणां यत् एतत् कदनं कृतम्, तत् का अन्या प्रकरोति?
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause in the passive (यत् … कदनं त्वया कृतम्), with the absolutive phrase (रूपैः … कृत्वा) giving the means; the main clause is a rhetorical question resuming it with तत्.
mantras.lit: This slaughter of the great asuras, haters of dharma, which was wrought by you today, O Devī, having made your own body manifold through many forms — O Ambikā, what other (woman) does that?
mantras.tr: Today, Devī, you made your own form manifold in many shapes and wrought this slaughter of the great asuras who hated dharma. Ambikā, who else could do such a thing?
mantras.tr_note: The passive is turned active; the rhetorical present प्रकरोति is rendered ‘could do’.

comm.t: The gods recall the battle of chapters 8–10: the Devī appeared as many — the Mātṛkās, Kālī, Śivadūtī — and destroyed the asuras. No other being could have done it.

The stanza answers Śumbha’s taunt that she fought ‘relying on the strength of others’ (10.3 अन्यासां बलमाश्रित्य). The Devī had replied that the many forms were her own powers and drew them back into herself: एकैवाहं जगत्यत्र द्वितीया का ममापरा (10.5), ‘I alone am here in the world; who else is there besides me?’, and ‘I stood here in many forms by my power’ (10.8 अहं विभूत्या बहुभिरिह रूपैर्यदास्थिता). The gods’ question का अन्या echoes her own द्वितीया का.
A modern reading: plurality here is not division. The many forms are one power acting in many ways.

morph.note: Causative of √भ्रम् ‘to wander, whirl’: the root vowel takes vṛddhi before -अय- (भ्रम् → भ्रामय-), ‘makes wander’; with वि ‘astray, about’. Its subject is का त्वदन्या, third person — so the question of the second line runs on into the second half: ‘who but you makes this world whirl?’.
ममत्व is an abstract noun in -त्व formed on मम, the genitive ‘of me, mine’: ‘mine-ness’, possessiveness. Abstracts formed on a case-form are rare and expressive.
