mantras.anvaya: विद्यासु शास्त्रेषु विवेकदीपेषु आद्येषु वाक्येषु च त्वदन्या का (वर्तते)? अतिमहान्धकारे ममत्वगर्ते एतत् विश्वम् अतीव (त्वदन्या का) विभ्रामयति?
mantras.anvaya_en: One rhetorical question (का त्वदन्या) governs both halves: in the first it is the subject of an understood ‘is’ with five locatives; in the second it is the subject of विभ्रामयति.
mantras.lit: In the branches of knowledge, in the śāstras, in the primal sayings that are lamps of discernment — who is there other than you? (Who other than you) makes this universe whirl exceedingly in the pit of possessiveness, of very great darkness?
mantras.tr: In all knowledge and every scripture, in the ancient words that are lamps of discernment, who is there but you? And who but you sets this whole world whirling in the dark abyss of ‘mine’?
mantras.tr_note: The question का त्वदन्या is carried into the second half, as the third-person verb requires.

comm.t: Two sides of one power. The Goddess is present in every source of knowledge and discernment; and it is she who sends the world whirling in the darkness of possessiveness. The same question, ‘who but you?’, covers both.

The teaching is Medhas’s in the first chapter: creatures are thrown ‘into the whirlpool of mine-ness, the pit of delusion’ (1.53 ममतावर्त्ते मोहगर्ते निपातिताः) by the power of Mahāmāyā, who drags even the minds of the wise into delusion (1.55–56) and is also the supreme knowledge that frees (1.57). The ‘primal sayings’ are commonly understood as the Vedas. The question का त्वदन्या was asked in the gods’ hymn of chapter 4 as well (4.17).

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) holds both sides in two names: विश्वभ्रमणकारिणी (name 889), ‘she who makes the universe whirl’, and ममताहन्त्री (name 165), ‘destroyer of possessiveness’. The texts are separate; the paired idea is shared.
A modern reading: the pit is ‘mine’. What darkens the world in this stanza is not ignorance of facts but the habit of possession.

mantras.anvaya_en: A series of relative clauses of place (यत्र …) with the verb ‘to be’ understood, closed by the correlative तत्र and the main clause.
mantras.lit: Where there are rākṣasas, where serpents of fierce venom, where enemies, where bands of robbers, where a forest fire, and likewise in the midst of the ocean — standing there, you protect the world.
mantras.tr: Where demons are, and serpents of deadly venom, where enemies and robber bands, where the forest is ablaze, and out on the open sea — there you stand and guard the world.

comm.t: A catalogue of the dangers of the wild and of travel: demons, snakes, enemies, robbers, fire, the sea. Wherever danger is, the Goddess is there (तत्र स्थिता) and protects. The repeated यत्र, four times in three lines, builds the list.

The Devī makes the matching promise in chapter 12: one who remembers her story is freed from distress when surrounded by forest fire, beset by robbers or held by enemies, or tossed by the wind ‘in a ship on the great ocean’ (12.25–29 दावाग्निपरिवारितः … दस्युभिर्वा वृतः … स्थितः पोते महार्णवे).
A modern reading: the hymn does not say she removes every danger from the world, but that she stands within it. Protection is presence.

mantras.anvaya: हे विश्वेश्वरि, त्वं विश्वं परिपासि। (त्वं) विश्वात्मिका (असि) इति विश्वं धारयसि। भवती विश्वेशवन्द्या (अस्ति)। ये त्वयि भक्तिनम्राः, (ते) विश्वाश्रयाः भवन्ति।
mantras.anvaya_en: Four short statements, one to a line: she protects; being its self she sustains; she is revered by its lords; her devotees become its refuge.
mantras.lit: O Queen of the universe, you protect the universe; being the self of the universe, therefore you uphold the universe. Your Ladyship is to be revered by the lords of the universe; those who are bowed in devotion to you become the refuges of the universe.
mantras.tr: Queen of the universe, you guard the universe; as its very self you hold the universe up. The lords of the universe revere you, and those who bow to you in devotion become the shelter of the universe.

comm.t: The word विश्व ‘universe’ is struck six times in four lines. She protects the universe, sustains it because it is her own self, is honoured by its rulers, and makes her devotees its refuge. The last line takes up 11.29: those who take refuge in her become a refuge (आश्रयतां प्रयान्ति).

The thought that she holds the world because she is its self is Brahmā’s in the first carita (1.75 त्वयैतद्धार्यते विश्वं), and the gods opened this hymn with the same title (11.3 प्रसीद विश्वेश्वरि पाहि विश्वम्). ‘The lords of the universe’ are the ruling gods, who, as Brahmā says, took their bodies through her (1.84–85).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has विश्वधारिणी (name 759), ‘she who upholds the universe’. A shared idea; separate works.

mantras.anvaya_en: Three imperatives. The second is qualified by a comparison (यथा … सद्यः) whose verb is understood; the third has two objects joined by च and the goal प्रशमम्.
mantras.lit: O Devī, be gracious; protect us always from the fear of enemies, as (you did) just now, at once, through the slaying of the asuras; lead quickly to extinction the sins of all the worlds and the great calamities born of the ripening of portents.
mantras.tr: Be gracious, Devī. Guard us always from fear of our foes, as you did just now, at once, by slaying the asuras. Swiftly bring to rest the sins of all the worlds and the great calamities that ripen from evil portents.
mantras.tr_note: ‘as you did’ supplies the verb implied by यथा; ‘our’ is supplied with ‘foes’.

comm.t: The last long stanza of the hymn, in vasantatilakā (fourteen syllables a line), the metre of the gods’ hymn in chapter 4, which also opened a stanza with देवि प्रसीद (4.14). The gods ask for continued protection, citing what she has just done, and for the calming of sin and calamity in every world.

The Devī herself promises the same in chapter 12: hearing her story ‘would quell all calamities born of plague, and the threefold portent’ (12.8 उपसर्गानशेषांस्तु महामारीसमुद्भवान्। तथा त्रिविधमुत्पातं माहात्म्यं शमयेन्मम), and she prescribes its hearing in every rite of pacification (12.16–17). The prayer of chapter 11 and the promise of chapter 12 answer each other.
A modern reading: ‘as you did just now’ — the prayer rests on remembered help. Gratitude for the past becomes trust for the future.

त्रैलोक्य ‘the three worlds’ is a taddhita (with vṛddhi of the first vowel) from त्रिलोक; वासिन् ‘dweller’ is an agent noun of √वस् ‘to dwell’.

mantras.anvaya: हे विश्वार्तिहारिणि त्रैलोक्यवासिनाम् ईड्ये देवि, त्वं प्रणतानां प्रसीद, लोकानां वरदा भव।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two imperatives addressed to one subject (त्वम्), each with a genitive of the persons concerned (प्रणतानाम्, लोकानाम्); three vocatives name her.
mantras.lit: Be gracious, you, to those who bow down, O Devī, remover of the world’s affliction; O you who are to be praised by the dwellers of the three worlds, be the giver of boons to the worlds.
mantras.tr: Be gracious to those who bow before you, Devī, who take away the sorrow of the world. Praised by all who dwell in the three worlds, be the giver of boons to all the worlds.

comm.t: The last verse of the gods’ hymn (the Nārāyaṇī Stuti, 11.3–35) returns to the anuṣṭubh and closes with a request: ‘be the giver of boons’ (वरदा भव). The Devī answers at once in the next verses with the same word: वरदाहं सुरगणा वरं यन्मनसेच्छथ (11.37), ‘I am the giver of boons, hosts of gods; choose the boon you wish’.

The hymn is framed by one prayer. It opened with देवि प्रपन्नार्तिहरे प्रसीद (11.3), ‘O Devī who remove the affliction of those who take refuge, be gracious’, and it ends with प्रसीद … विश्वार्तिहारिणि: the remover of the suppliants’ pain is now the remover of the world’s.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name वरदा (name 331). A shared epithet; separate works.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) सुरगणाः, अहं वरदा (अस्मि)। यत् वरं मनसा इच्छथ, जगताम् उपकारकं तं वृणुध्वम्; (तं) प्रयच्छामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: A nominal sentence (अहं वरदा) and the address; then a relative clause (यत् वरं … इच्छथ) picked up by तम्, the object of the imperative वृणुध्वम्; प्रयच्छामि closes with an implied object.
mantras.lit: I am the giver of boons, O hosts of gods. The boon which you desire in your mind — choose that, beneficial to the worlds; I grant it.
mantras.tr: I am the giver of boons, you hosts of gods. Choose the boon your minds desire, one that will benefit the worlds, and I shall grant it.
mantras.tr_note: The object of प्रयच्छामि is supplied (‘it’), and the present is rendered as a promise (‘I shall grant’).

comm.t: Pleased by the hymn, the Goddess offers a boon, as she did after the hymn of chapter 4 (4.32). She sets one condition herself: the boon is to be जगताम् उपकारकम्, of benefit to the worlds, not to the gods alone.

Each of the text’s great hymns is followed by a boon (1.95–98 to Viṣṇu from the asuras, 4.32–37 and here). In the Śākta reading the pattern teaches that praise is answered: the Goddess is वरदा, the one who grants what is asked.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) gives the same epithet as a name: 331, वरदा. Here it is the Goddess’s own word for herself in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa; the shared title is a shared Śākta idea, not a borrowing between the texts.

flags.uncertain: यत् … तम्: the relative is neuter and the correlative masculine. Read here as a generic ‘whatever (boon)’; it may also be a loose agreement for यम्. The sense is the same either way.

morph.note: Gerundive of √कृ with ṇyat (कृ + य, vṛddhi → कार्य): ‘to be done’. The agent goes in the instrumental (त्वया), the thing to be done is the grammatical subject; neuter singular agrees with प्रशमनम् and विनाशनम् taken together as one task.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) अखिलेश्वरि, त्रैलोक्यस्य सर्वाबाधाप्रशमनम् (तथा) अस्मद्वैरिविनाशनम् एवम् एव त्वया कार्यम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A passive construction with the gerundive: the two nouns of action are the subjects, कार्यम् the predicate, त्वया the agent; एवम् एव points back to what she has just done.
mantras.lit: O Queen of all, the quelling of all afflictions of the three worlds — and in just this way the destruction of our enemies — is to be done by you.
mantras.tr: O Sovereign of all, quell every affliction of the three worlds, and destroy our enemies just as you have done now.
mantras.tr_note: The gerundive (‘is to be done by you’) is rendered as a request; ‘as you have done now’ interprets एवम् एव, ‘in just this way’.

comm.t: The gods ask for two things: that every affliction of the three worlds be quelled, and that their enemies be destroyed एवम् एव, ‘in just this way’ — as Śumbha and Niśumbha have just been. They ask not for one deliverance but for a standing promise.
The request matches the Goddess’s own condition in 11.37: the boon is for the three worlds, not for the gods alone. Her answer (11.41–55) turns it into the prophecy of her future descents.

comm.t: The Goddess grants the gods’ request. What follows (11.41–55) is her prophecy: the future forms in which she will come down to destroy the enemies of the worlds. The speech runs to the end of the chapter; chapter 12 continues it with the fruits of hearing the text.

mantras.anvaya_en: Time is given by a locative absolute (वैवस्वते अन्तरे प्राप्ते) and a locative (अष्टाविंशतिमे युगे); the subject is the pair शुम्भः निशुम्भः च with अन्यौ and महासुरौ; the verb is the dual future उत्पत्स्येते.
mantras.lit: When the Vaivasvata manvantara has come, in the twenty-eighth yuga, two others, Śumbha and Niśumbha, great asuras, will arise.
mantras.tr: In the age of Vaivasvata Manu, in its twenty-eighth cycle, two other great asuras named Śumbha and Niśumbha will be born.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Cycle’ renders युग, which here means a whole round of four ages; ‘named’ interprets अन्यौ: a second pair bearing the same names.

comm.t: The prophecy begins with a date. The present story is set long before; the Goddess now looks ahead to the seventh manvantara, that of Vaivasvata Manu, and to its twenty-eighth great cycle, when a second Śumbha and Niśumbha will be born. Her answer to the gods’ request (11.39) is a promise to return.

In Purāṇic reckoning the present world-age is the twenty-eighth great cycle of the Vaivasvata manvantara, the cycle in which Kṛṣṇa was born. The next verse confirms the setting: the Goddess will be born in Nanda’s house.

mantras.anvaya_en: The subject is the ‘I’ of the verb; the three feminine nominatives (जाता, यशोदागर्भसम्भवा, विन्ध्याचलनिवासिनी) describe her; ततः तौ नाशयिष्यामि is the main clause.
mantras.lit: Born in the house of Nanda the cowherd, born from the womb of Yaśodā, then, dwelling on the Vindhya mountain, I shall destroy those two.
mantras.tr: Born in the house of Nanda the cowherd, from the womb of Yaśodā, I shall then dwell on the Vindhya mountain and destroy them both.
mantras.tr_note: The participial nominative विन्ध्याचलनिवासिनी is turned into a finite clause (‘I shall dwell’).

comm.t: The first future form: the Goddess will be born to Yaśodā in the house of Nanda the cowherd, and, dwelling on the Vindhya hills, will slay the second Śumbha and Niśumbha. The text names no new name here; the epithet विन्ध्याचलनिवासिनी serves as one.

This is the daughter of Yaśodā whom the Purāṇic Kṛṣṇa story (Harivaṃśa, Bhāgavata) tells of: exchanged for the infant Kṛṣṇa, she escapes the hands of Kaṃsa and goes to dwell on the Vindhya. The tradition identifies her with Yogamāyā and with Vindhyavāsinī, still worshipped on the Vindhya hills.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the identical compound as a name: 336, विन्ध्याचलनिवासिनी. The two texts are distinct; they share the cult of the Vindhya Goddess.

mantras.anvaya: पुनः अपि अतिरौद्रेण रूपेण पृथिवीतले अवतीर्य (अहं) वैप्रचित्तान् दानवान् तु हनिष्यामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: The absolutive अवतीर्य, with its manner (अतिरौद्रेण रूपेण) and place (पृथिवीतले), precedes the main verb हनिष्यामि and its object वैप्रचित्तान् दानवान्.
mantras.lit: Yet again, having descended in an exceedingly terrible form onto the surface of the earth, I shall slay the Dānavas, the descendants of Vipracitti.
mantras.tr: And again, descending to earth in a form of utter ferocity, I shall slay the Dānavas born of Vipracitti.

comm.t: The second descent. The Goddess will come down to earth in a most terrible form to kill the Vaipracittas, the Dānava descendants of Vipracitti. The verb अवतीर्य, ‘having descended’, names what the whole passage describes: her avatāras.
The form is named only in the next verse, from its result: her teeth will be red as pomegranate flowers, and she will be called Raktadantikā (11.44–45).

samasa.sense: red as pomegranate blossoms
samasa.alt: उपम may also be taken as the adjective ‘like’, giving a tatpuruṣa दाडिमीकुसुमैः उपमाः ‘comparable to pomegranate flowers’; the sense is the same.

morph.note: Present participle of the curādi stem भक्षय-: भक्षयत्, feminine भक्षयन्ती (with the nasal), genitive singular -याः. It refers to the speaker: ‘of (me) devouring’, so ‘my teeth’.
Past participle of √रञ्ज्, the nasal lost and j → k before t (रक्त), used as the adjective ‘red’.

mantras.anvaya: तान् उग्रान् वैप्रचित्तान् महासुरान् भक्षयन्त्याः च (मम) दन्ताः दाडिमीकुसुमोपमाः रक्ताः भविष्यन्ति।
mantras.anvaya_en: The genitive participial phrase (भक्षयन्त्याः … महासुरान्) gives the owner of the teeth; the main clause is दन्ताः रक्ताः भविष्यन्ति with the comparison दाडिमीकुसुमोपमाः.
mantras.lit: And of (me) as I devour those fierce Vaipracitta great asuras, the teeth will become red, like pomegranate flowers.
mantras.tr: And as I devour those fierce great asuras of Vipracitti’s line, my teeth will turn red, like the flowers of the pomegranate.
mantras.tr_note: ‘My’ renders the genitive feminine participle, which refers to the speaker.

comm.t: The terrible form of 11.43 devours the Vaipracittas, and her teeth are stained red like pomegranate flowers. The simile is visual and exact: the red of the blossom, not of blood, is the image the text chooses.

The feature gives the form its name in the next verse, Raktadantikā, ‘the Red-toothed’. The devouring recalls Cāmuṇḍā (Kālī) in the Raktabīja battle, told to range the field ‘devouring’ the asuras born of his blood — the same participle, भक्षयन्ती (8.55; the battle 8.53–61).

mantras.anvaya: ततः स्वर्गे देवताः मर्त्यलोके च मानवाः स्तुवन्तः मां सततं रक्तदन्तिकां व्याहरिष्यन्ति।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two subjects with their places (स्वर्गे देवताः, मर्त्यलोके मानवाः), the participle स्तुवन्तः, the verb व्याहरिष्यन्ति with object (माम्) and predicate accusative (रक्तदन्तिकाम्).
mantras.lit: Therefore the deities in heaven and the humans in the world of mortals, praising me, will constantly call me Raktadantikā.
mantras.tr: So the gods in heaven and men on earth will praise me and call me ever by the name Raktadantikā, the Red-toothed.
mantras.tr_note: ‘The Red-toothed’ glosses the name; ‘by the name’ makes the double accusative explicit.

comm.t: The second form receives its name: Raktadantikā, ‘she whose teeth are red’. Gods in heaven and humans on earth will both use it — the prophecy names the worshippers as well as the form.

The Mūrtirahasya, one of the three rahasyas recited after the Saptaśatī in the Gita Press pāṭha, describes the future forms of this passage for meditation, Raktadantikā among them. In the chapter itself she is known only by what these two verses say.

mantras.anvaya: भूयः च शतवार्षिक्याम् अनम्भसि अनावृष्ट्यां (सत्यां) मुनिभिः संस्तुता (अहम्) अयोनिजा भूमौ सम्भविष्यामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: The locatives give the occasion (a waterless hundred-year drought); मुनिभिः संस्तुता gives the cause; the main clause is (अहम्) अयोनिजा भूमौ सम्भविष्यामि.
mantras.lit: And again, in a drought lasting a hundred years, without water, praised by the sages, I shall come into being on the earth, not born from a womb.
mantras.tr: And once more, when the earth lies a hundred years without rain or water, I shall appear on earth at the sages’ praise, born of no womb.
mantras.tr_note: ‘At the sages’ praise’ renders मुनिभिः संस्तुता (‘praised by the sages’) as the occasion of her coming.

comm.t: The third descent begins: a drought of a hundred years, the sages praise her, and she appears on earth अयोनिजा, born of no mother. Unlike the daughter of Yaśodā (11.42), this form has no human birth.

Verses 11.46–50 are one episode with three names: Śatākṣī (11.47), Śākambharī (11.49) and Durgā (11.50), all of the same appearance (तत्रैव, ‘right there’, 11.49). The tradition treats them as one Goddess named by three of her deeds.

human beings

The neuter relative used as a conjunction, ‘since, because’, answered by ततः ‘therefore’ at the end of the verse: यत् … ततः.
Future of the curādi stem कीर्तय- (कीर्तय + इष्य + अन्ति); with माम् … शताक्षीम् इति, ‘they will proclaim me as Śatākṣī’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः यत् (अहं) नेत्राणां शतेन मुनीन् निरीक्षिष्यामि, ततः मनुजाः मां शताक्षीम् इति कीर्तयिष्यन्ति।
mantras.anvaya_en: A causal clause (यत् … निरीक्षिष्यामि) and its correlative main clause (ततः … कीर्तयिष्यन्ति); इति marks the name.
mantras.lit: Then, since I shall look upon the sages with a hundred eyes, men will therefore proclaim me as ‘Śatākṣī’.
mantras.tr: Because I shall look upon the sages with a hundred eyes, men will call me Śatākṣī, the Hundred-eyed.
mantras.tr_note: The first ततः (‘then’) is left untranslated in tr; ‘the Hundred-eyed’ glosses the name.

comm.t: The first name of the third descent: she looks upon the sages with a hundred eyes, and so is called Śatākṣī. The text gives only the gaze; it does not say what the eyes do.

Later Śākta retellings fill the gap. In the Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa the Hundred-eyed Goddess, seeing the suffering of the drought, weeps from all her eyes, and her tears become the rain that refills the rivers. The Devī Māhātmya itself says only that she looked.
A modern reading: the first thing the Goddess does in the famine is to see. Attention comes before relief.

flags.uncertain: यत्: read as the conjunction ‘since’, answered by ततः. It could also be taken as ‘when’ (‘when I look upon the sages …’); the sense is nearly the same.

samasa.sense: life-sustaining

morph.note: Future of √भृ: roots in ṛ take the connecting vowel i in the future (भर् + इष्य + आमि). ‘I shall bear, sustain’ — the verb from which the name Śākambharī (11.49) is made.
आ (आङ्) with the ablative marks a limit: आ वृष्टेः ‘until the rain’. The text writes it joined (आवृष्टेः); it is not a compound, since वृष्टेः keeps its own case ending.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) सुराः, ततः अहम् आ वृष्टेः आत्मदेहसमुद्भवैः प्राणधारकैः शाकैः अखिलं लोकं भरिष्यामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject अहम्, verb भरिष्यामि, object अखिलं लोकम्; the instrument शाकैः with two epithets; आ वृष्टेः gives the limit of time.
mantras.lit: Then I, O gods, shall sustain the whole world, until the rain, with life-sustaining vegetables arisen from my own body.
mantras.tr: Then, O gods, until the rains return, I shall feed the whole world with life-giving plants grown from my own body.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Until the rains return’ renders आ वृष्टेः, ‘until the rain’; ‘feed’ renders भरिष्यामि, ‘sustain, nourish’.

comm.t: In the drought the Goddess feeds the world from her own body: edible plants that keep life going until the rain comes. The verse prepares her name in 11.49, Śākambharī, ‘she who bears (the world with) vegetables’.

The image of the Goddess as the one who feeds is old in Śākta devotion: Śākambharī is worshipped as the giver of food in famine. The verse itself is precise about the limit — आ वृष्टेः, only until the rain — the Goddess sustains, and the ordinary order resumes.

flags.uncertain: The printed आवृष्टेः is divided here as आ + वृष्टेः (‘until the rain’), the reading of the usual translations. Taking आवृष्टि as one noun (‘rainfall’, ablative ‘from the rain’) makes poorer sense of the verse.

mantras.anvaya: तदा अहं भुवि शाकम्भरी इति विख्यातिं यास्यामि। तत्र एव च दुर्गमाख्यं महासुरं वधिष्यामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: (1) अहं … विख्यातिं यास्यामि with the name in an इति phrase; (2) तत्र एव च … वधिष्यामि with its object.
mantras.lit: Then I shall go to renown on earth as ‘Śākambharī’; and right there I shall slay the great asura named Durgama.
mantras.tr: Then I shall be famed on earth as Śākambharī, and in that same descent I shall slay the great asura called Durgama.
mantras.tr_note: ‘In that same descent’ interprets तत्र एव, ‘right there’.

comm.t: The second name of the third descent: Śākambharī, ‘she who sustains with plants’, from the deed of 11.48. In the same appearance (तत्र एव) she slays a great asura named Durgama, whose name gives her third name in 11.50.

The text says nothing more of Durgama. Later Śākta retellings, such as the Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa, make him the cause of the drought: having taken the Vedas from the gods by a boon, he stopped the sacrifices, and the rains failed. The Devī Māhātmya gives only the name and the slaying.

samasa.alt: Also analysed as a karmadhāraya with the middle member dropped, हिमयुक्तः अचलः ‘the snowy mountain’; the referent is the same.

morph.note: The name is given from the deed of 11.49: she who slew Durgama is called Durgā. As a word, दुर्ग (दुस् + √गम्, ‘hard to reach’) with the feminine -ā; the text connects it with the asura’s name, not with this etymology.

mantras.anvaya: ‘दुर्गा देवी’ इति तत् मे नाम विख्यातं भविष्यति। पुनः च यदा अहं हिमाचले भीमं रूपं कृत्वा (11.51: रक्षांसि भक्षयिष्यामि …)
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line closes the third descent: तत् मे नाम (subject) विख्यातं भविष्यति, with the name in an इति phrase. The second line opens a new यदा-clause (the fourth descent) whose verb is in 11.51.
mantras.lit: ‘Durgā Devī’ — thus that name of mine will become renowned. And again, when I, having assumed a terrible form on the Himālaya, —
mantras.tr: That name of mine, Durgā Devī, will be renowned. And again, when I take a terrible form on the Himālaya,
mantras.tr_note: The second line is the beginning of a sentence completed in 11.51–52.

comm.t: The third name of the same descent: having slain Durgama (11.49), the Goddess will be known as Durgā Devī. The second line opens the fourth descent: a terrible form on the Himālaya, completed in the next verse.

Here the text explains the name Durgā by a deed — the slaying of Durgama — not by the meaning ‘hard to approach’. The name has been used of her throughout the Devī Māhātmya; the prophecy gives it its story.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has दुर्गमा and दुर्गा as consecutive names, 189 and 190. The pairing is shared Śākta vocabulary; the Sahasranāma does not tell the story of Durgama.

mantras.lit: — shall devour the rākṣasas for the protection of the sages, then all the sages, with bodies bowed low, will praise me;
mantras.tr: and devour the rākṣasas to protect the sages, then all the sages will bow low and praise me,
mantras.tr_note: The participial compound आनम्रमूर्तयः is rendered as a verb (‘bow low’). The sentence runs from 11.50 to 11.52.

comm.t: The fourth descent: on the Himālaya, in a terrible form, the Goddess devours rākṣasas to protect the sages, and the sages bow and praise her. The name follows in 11.52.
As in the third descent, the occasion is the sages’ need; each form in this prophecy is called down by a particular distress and named by those it saves.

grievous oppression of the worlds

mantras.anvaya: (तदा) ‘भीमा देवी’ इति तत् मे नाम विख्यातं भविष्यति। यदा अरुणाख्यः त्रैलोक्ये महाबाधां करिष्यति, (11.53: तदा अहं …)
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line closes the sentence of 11.50–51 with the name; the second opens the fifth descent with a यदा-clause whose correlative is in 11.53.
mantras.lit: ‘Bhīmā Devī’ — thus that name of mine will become renowned. When the one named Aruṇa causes great affliction in the three worlds, —
mantras.tr: and my name will be renowned as Bhīmā Devī. When the asura called Aruṇa brings great oppression on the three worlds,
mantras.tr_note: ‘Asura’ is supplied; the text gives only the name Aruṇa, but 11.53 calls him महासुरम्.

comm.t: The fourth form is named: Bhīmā Devī, ‘the Terrible Goddess’, from the terrible form of 11.50. The second line opens the fifth and last named descent: an asura called Aruṇa will afflict the three worlds.
The line ‘… इति विख्यातं तन्मे नाम भविष्यति’ is repeated word for word from 11.50, a formula that seals each naming. The repeated formula is how the prophecy keeps its shape as a list of names.

mantras.lit: — then I, having assumed a bee-form of countless six-footed ones, shall slay the great asura for the welfare of the three worlds.
mantras.tr: then I shall take a form of countless bees and slay that great asura for the good of the three worlds.

comm.t: The fifth descent: against Aruṇa the Goddess takes a form made of innumerable bees and kills him for the welfare of the three worlds. The form is a swarm, not a single body.

Later Śākta retellings, such as the Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa, explain the form: Aruṇa had a boon that no two- or four-footed creature could kill him, so the Goddess came as six-footed bees. The Devī Māhātmya itself gives no reason for the form.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line closes the fifth descent with the name; the second begins the closing generalisation, a distributive यदा यदा-clause whose correlative तदा तदा is in 11.55.
mantras.lit: And then the people everywhere will praise me as ‘Bhrāmarī’. Thus, whenever affliction arising from the Dānavas shall occur, —
mantras.tr: and people everywhere will then praise me as Bhrāmarī. Thus, whenever oppression born of the demons arises,
mantras.tr_note: ‘Demons’ renders दानव (the sons of Danu); the sentence is completed in 11.55.

comm.t: The fifth form is named: Bhrāmarī, ‘she of the bees’, praised everywhere. With इत्थम्, ‘thus’, the Goddess turns from the list of named descents to a rule: whenever demons cause affliction.

After the daughter of Yaśodā (11.42) the prophecy has named six forms in four descents: Raktadantikā; Śatākṣī, Śākambharī and Durgā (one descent, 11.46–50); Bhīmā; and Bhrāmarī. The Mūrtirahasya recited after the Saptaśatī gives meditations on these forms.

samasa.sense: the ending of the foes (of the worlds and the gods)

morph.note: Repetition for distribution (vīpsā): यदा यदा … तदा तदा ‘whenever … each time then’. The doubled word makes a single promise into a standing rule.
Future of √कृ with iṭ (कर् + इष्य + आमि). With अरिसंक्षयम्, ‘I shall make an end of the enemies’ — the last verb of the chapter.

mantras.anvaya: (यदा यदा दानवोत्था बाधा भविष्यति,) तदा तदा अहम् अवतीर्य अरिसंक्षयं करिष्यामि॥
mantras.anvaya_en: The correlative clause of 11.54b: the doubled तदा तदा, the absolutive अवतीर्य, the verb करिष्यामि and its object.
mantras.lit: — then, each time, having descended, I shall bring about the destruction of the enemies.
mantras.tr: each time I shall descend and destroy the enemies.
mantras.tr_note: The half-śloka completes the sentence begun in 11.54; ‘each time’ renders the doubled तदा.

comm.t: The prophecy closes in a rule: whenever demons afflict the worlds, the Goddess will descend (अवतीर्य) and destroy the enemies. This answers the gods’ request of 11.39 exactly: एवम् एव, ‘in just this way’, every time. A half-śloka, counted by the Gita Press as its own mantra; the closing ॐ belongs to the recitation.

The construction recalls the Bhagavadgītā’s promise of descent (4.7–8, यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य …): the same यदा यदा and the same idea of a recurring descent. Here the one who descends is the Goddess, and the occasion is the oppression of the worlds by demons.
A modern reading: the chapter ends not with a final victory but with a promise of return. The text treats protection as a pattern that repeats, not a single event.
